title: Spanish foundations
description: One hundred and six Spanish lessons in twenty-six units. Units 1-12 (35 lessons, CEFR A1) cover first words, introductions, café requests, numbers, directions, shopping, time and days, family, home and daily routine, everyday exchanges, getting around, past and future plans, weather and time-telling, months and dates, the market, free time, health and social life. Units 13-17 (17 lessons, CEFR A2) add five units — El pasado (preterite, imperfect, choosing between them, weekend narratives), El futuro (future formation and uses, plans and intentions), Deseos y cortesía (conditional, polite requests, first subjunctive), Conectar frases (relative clauses, comparatives, object pronouns, por vs para), and Trabajo y tecnología (superlatives, a hotel check-in mission, tech talk). Units 18-20 (18 lessons) are a B1-oriented pilot — Viaje interrumpido (travel disruption), El trabajo y los estudios (work and study plans), Una decisión social (a social decision) — with three extended readings, three multi-minute listenings, hosted multi-turn dialogues, connected writing and speaking tasks; it is B1-oriented practice, not a claim that completing it confers B1. Units 21-23 (18 lessons) extend the B1-oriented path — Historias que cuento (personal accounts), Planes y consecuencias (plans and consequences), Opiniones con razones (opinions with reasons) — a narrative-to-argumentative arc with two more multi-minute listenings, one extended reading, three hosted multi-turn dialogues, connected writing and voice-note speaking tasks; like units 18-20, it is B1-oriented practice, not a claim that completing it confers B1. Units 24-25 (12 lessons) continue the B1-oriented path — Problemas cotidianos (everyday practical problems) and Seguir el hilo (following a longer thread) — with two more multi-minute listenings, one extended reading, two hosted multi-turn dialogues, connected writing and voice-note speaking tasks, and the pack's independent checkpoint, which surfaces at the end of this extended path; like units 18-23, it is B1-oriented practice, not a claim that completing it confers B1. Unit 26 (6 lessons) is a B2-oriented pilot — Ponerse en el otro lado (taking the other side) — with connective signpost work, an extended reading that presents two positions, a multi-minute two-voice listening, a hosted mediation dialogue, a connected writing argument with a counterpoint, and a voice-note speaking task; it is B2-oriented practice, not a claim that completing it confers B2. CEFR level tagging is partial, and native-speaker editorial review remains open for the whole pack; lessons are machine-authored and consistency-checked.

units.title: Meeting people
units.objective: Introduce yourself and your family.

units.title: Getting around
units.objective: Understand prices and quantities in everyday errands.

units.title: Finding your way
units.objective: Ask where things are and follow spoken directions.

units.title: Everyday life
units.objective: Talk about days, times, and the people around you.

units.title: En acción
units.objective: Use your Spanish in new ways: build, decide, remember.

units.title: De nuevo
units.objective: Use your Spanish in new ways: complete missions and build sentences.

units.title: En casa y a diario
units.objective: Talk about your home and your day in Spanish.

units.title: Comunicación diaria
units.objective: Handle everyday exchanges: no, questions, food, mine and yours.

units.title: Más lejos
units.objective: Go further: move around, ask politely, talk about yesterday and tomorrow.

units.title: El tiempo y el mundo
units.objective: Master time words, the weather, and the market.

units.title: Tiempo libre
units.objective: Talk about what you love doing.

units.title: Salud y vida social
units.objective: Take care of yourself and your social life in Spanish.

units.title: El pasado
units.objective: Talk about what happened: the preterite and the imperfect.

units.title: El futuro
units.objective: Talk about tomorrow: the simple future and your plans.

units.title: Deseos y cortesía
units.objective: Wish, ask politely, and trigger the subjunctive.

units.title: Conectar frases
units.objective: Link ideas: relative clauses, comparisons, pronouns, por and para.

units.title: Trabajo y tecnología
units.objective: Work, superlatives, the hotel mission, and tech talk.

units.title: Viaje interrumpido
units.objective: Handle a disrupted trip: retell what happened, understand a station or airport announcement, rebook with an agent, and follow up in writing.

units.title: El trabajo y los estudios
units.objective: Talk about work and study plans and intentions, follow a job- or study-related conversation, and justify decisions with reasons.

units.title: Una decisión social
units.objective: Negotiate a social decision: explain a preference with a reason, accept or decline gracefully, and agree on a plan.

units.title: Historias que cuento
units.objective: Recount a personal story in connected sentences, say what people told you, react to someone else's account, and retell it to a new listener.

units.title: Planes y consecuencias
units.objective: State a plan, say what it depends on, and explain consequences - anticipated and actual - with causal and consequence frames.

units.title: Opiniones con razones
units.objective: Give an opinion with a reason and a supporting detail, agree and disagree politely, and follow a longer spoken discussion of opinions.

units.title: Problemas cotidianos
units.objective: Describe a practical everyday problem clearly, ask for a solution politely, negotiate a fix in a branched exchange, and leave a clear message that resolves the problem with a new listener.

units.title: Seguir el hilo
units.objective: Follow a longer spoken piece and a longer written text, keep track of the thread across sections, clarify when you lose it, and summarise or relay the gist to someone new.

units.title: Ponerse en el otro lado
units.objective: Follow a longer discussion and a longer article that present two positions, notice and use the signposts of an argument, concede and counter with contrastive connectives, mediate a disagreement, and write an argued position with an answered counterpoint.

concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: Spanish greets by the hour, and it greets in the plural even for a single morning: buenos días, buenas tardes. The habit worth starting on day one is that Spanish marks a question twice, with an upside-down question mark at the front and an ordinary one at the end, so you can see a question coming before you have read a word of it.

examples.meaning: Hello.
Thank you.

concepts.commonError: Say hola the moment you arrive. Save adiós for leaving.

concepts.title: Introducing yourself
concepts.explanation: Spanish says Me llamo Ana, literally 'I call myself Ana'; the verb llamarse carries a pronoun that points back at the speaker. Asking the same question of someone else changes that pronoun to te: ¿Cómo te llamas? Soy Ana is the plain alternative, built on 'to be'.

examples.meaning: My name is Ana.
What is your name?
Nice to meet you.

concepts.commonError: Use me llamo for your own name and te llamas in the informal question. Do not swap me and te.

concepts.title: Polite café requests
concepts.explanation: For a polite café request Spanish uses quisiera, 'I would like', instead of the blunter quiero: Quisiera un café, por favor. The article stays un for either drink, and café and té keep their accents.

examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.
I would like a tea, please.
A coffee, please.

concepts.commonError: Keep un with café and té in these requests. Remember the accents in café and té.

concepts.title: Numbers and quantities
concepts.explanation: Spanish runs one to ten as ordinary digits, then glues the parts of a number together where English keeps them apart: dieciséis for sixteen, veintiuno for twenty-one. That gluing stops at thirty, where a separate y appears, treinta y uno. A number in front of a noun also has to agree with it: un café is one coffee, but una manzana is one apple.

examples.meaning: One, two, three, four, five.
How much does a coffee cost?
Two apples, please.

concepts.commonError: Use cuánto for the price of one item. Keep una with manzana because it is feminine.

concepts.title: Asking the way
concepts.explanation: Spanish marks the asking word with a written accent: dónde asks 'where', while the same letters without it, donde, are not asking anything. The accent does not change how the word sounds; it tells you what the word is doing, and a direct question also opens with ¿ and closes with ?. Ask about a place with estar, ¿Dónde está la estación?, and learn the directions as chunks: todo recto, a la izquierda, a la derecha, with luego joining the second step to the first.

examples.meaning: Where is the station?

examples.target: Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.
examples.meaning: Straight ahead, then to the left.
Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

concepts.commonError: Dónde asks where. Quién asks who and qué asks what. The accent on dónde marks the question and drops in the middle of a sentence.

concepts.title: Prices and paying
concepts.explanation: A Spanish question wears two marks, an upside-down one at the front and an ordinary one at the end, so ¿Cuánto cuesta? announces itself before you read a word. Costar changes its stem under stress: cuesta for a single item, cuestan for several, and never costa. The bill is la cuenta, a feminine noun, and por favor is the politeness that travels with it.

examples.meaning: How much does the coffee cost?
This is very expensive.
The bill, please.

concepts.commonError: Spanish puts no before the verb, never after it. Cost is cuesta for one thing and cuestan for several.

concepts.title: Days and times
concepts.explanation: Five Spanish weekdays are the old sky names — lunes (moon), martes (Mars), miércoles (Mercury), jueves (Jupiter), viernes (Venus) — while sábado and domingo come from the Sabbath and the Lord’s day. They are masculine and lower-case, and the article el carries the meaning of ‘on’: el lunes. Mañana is tomorrow; la mañana is the morning.

examples.meaning: Today is Wednesday.
On Monday I work.
Tomorrow is Thursday.

concepts.commonError: Mañana is both tomorrow and morning. La mañana is the morning; mañana alone in a schedule usually means tomorrow.

concepts.title: Family and people
concepts.explanation: Spanish shows a noun's gender in its article — el hermano, la hermana — and hides an irregular verb under the simplest sentence: yo tengo, never yo tene. The possessive mi does not change with who is speaking; it changes with how many people are being counted, so mi hermana is one sister and mis hermanas is two, whoever the speaker is.

examples.meaning: I have a brother.
I have a sister.
My parents live in Madrid.

concepts.commonError: Tengo, not tene. Tener is irregular in the I form and it is the form you use most when talking about family.

concepts.title: Home and articles
concepts.explanation: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and the article shows it: el dormitorio, la cocina. In the plural the articles become los and las. Two little contractions do heavy work: a + el becomes al, as in voy al baño, and de + el becomes del, as in vengo del salón.

examples.meaning: The bedroom is small.
The kitchen is big.
I go to the bathroom.
I come from the living room.

concepts.commonError: Never write a el or de el — the contraction is obligatory: al baño, del salón.

concepts.title: Describing people and things
concepts.explanation: Ser describes what something is like: El libro es nuevo. The adjective copies the noun's gender and number — alto for a masculine noun, alta for a feminine one, altos and altas in the plural. Muy simply turns the volume up: muy grande.

examples.meaning: The book is new.
The house is big.
He is very tall.
They (feminine) are very small.

concepts.commonError: The adjective must match the noun it describes, not the speaker: una mesa nueva, never una mesa nuevo.

concepts.title: More than one
concepts.explanation: The plural is almost always one step: add -s after a vowel — libro becomes libros, mesa becomes mesas. After a consonant, add -es — flor becomes flores, and lápiz changes its z to c: lápices. The article changes too: el becomes los, la becomes las.

examples.meaning: the books
the tables
the flowers
the pencils

concepts.commonError: After a consonant the plural needs -es, never just -s: flores, not flors.

concepts.title: Work and daily routine
concepts.explanation: Most Spanish verbs are regular: drop the -ar and add -o for I, -a for he or she — trabajo, trabaja. Estudiar works the same way: estudio, estudia. The day divides into three parts with por: por la mañana, por la tarde, por la noche.

examples.meaning: I work in the morning.
I study in the afternoon.

examples.target: Mi hermano trabaja por la noche.
examples.meaning: My brother works at night.

concepts.commonError: Por la mañana is a fixed phrase — never en la mañana.

concepts.title: Saying no
concepts.explanation: To negate, put no directly before the verb: No trabajo. Spanish also loves negative words that team up with no: nunca (never), nada (nothing), nadie (nobody). No como nada is perfectly correct — the two negatives strengthen each other instead of cancelling out.

examples.meaning: I don't work.
He/She doesn't study.
I don't eat anything.
Nobody speaks Spanish.

concepts.commonError: No must stand before the verb — Trabajo no is not Spanish.

concepts.title: Asking questions
concepts.explanation: Question words carry a written accent that tells them apart from their twins: qué (what) versus que (that), dónde (where) versus donde (where, as a connector). After the question word, the verb usually comes before the subject: ¿Dónde trabaja Ana? ¿Qué estudias?

examples.meaning: What is your name?
Where do you live?
What do you eat?
When do you work?

concepts.commonError: The accent is the meaning: ¿Como te llamas? would read as I eat your name.

concepts.title: Food and drink
concepts.explanation: Comer and beber are regular -er verbs: como, comes, come; bebo, bebes, bebe. Liking works backwards in Spanish: instead of I like the bread, Spanish says the bread is pleasing to me — Me gusta el pan. With a plural noun the verb becomes plural too: Me gustan las frutas.

examples.meaning: I eat bread.
I drink water.
I like cheese.
I like fruit.

concepts.commonError: Gustar agrees with the thing liked, not with you: Me gusta el pan, never Me gusto el pan.

concepts.title: Mine and yours
concepts.explanation: Mi, tu and su sit before the noun and never change for gender: mi libro, mi casa. They do change for number: mis libros, tus casas. Su is the busy one — it can mean his, her, your (formal) or their, and context does the sorting.

examples.meaning: My house is big.
Your book is new.
His friends live here.
My parents work.

concepts.commonError: The possessive copies the noun's number, not the owner's: mis libros even though there is only one of me.

concepts.title: Getting around
concepts.explanation: Ir (to go) is irregular but tiny: voy, vas, va, vamos, van. The transport goes after en — en coche, en metro, en autobús — with one rebel: a pie, on foot. To say where, use a: Voy al centro, from al = a + el.

examples.meaning: I go downtown by subway.

examples.target: Va a la escuela a pie.
examples.meaning: He/She goes to school on foot.
We go by car.

concepts.commonError: Transport takes en, never con: en metro, not con metro.

concepts.title: Polite requests
concepts.explanation: Poder (can) and querer (want) are followed by the infinitive: Puedo ir, Quiero comer. Their forms: puedo, puedes, puede and quiero, quieres, quiere. For extra politeness, Spanish reaches for the conditional: Querría un café, por favor — I would like a coffee, please.

examples.meaning: Can you help me?
I want a coffee.
I would like the bill, please.
I can go tomorrow.

concepts.commonError: After poder and querer comes the plain infinitive — Puedo ir, never Puedo voy.

concepts.title: Yesterday: a first look at the past
concepts.explanation: The pretérito talks about finished actions: for -ar verbs add -é for I — hablé, trabajé, estudié. For -er and -ir verbs add -í — comí, viví. Then there's fue, which does double duty as was and went. Anchor it all with ayer (yesterday) and anoche (last night).

examples.meaning: Yesterday I spoke with Ana.
I ate bread.
The party was good.
Last night I studied.

concepts.commonError: The accent is the past: hablo is I speak, hablé is I spoke.

concepts.title: Making plans
concepts.explanation: The near future is simply ir a plus the infinitive: Voy a cocinar, Vas a venir, Van a estudiar. It works for tonight, tomorrow, or next year — Spanish doesn't fuss about how near near is. Pair it with time words like mañana or este fin de semana.

examples.meaning: I'm going to cook.
We're going to travel.
Are you going to come?
They're going to study.

concepts.commonError: The a is not optional: Voy cocinar is missing its bridge — Voy a cocinar.

concepts.title: Weather and seasons
concepts.explanation: Spanish makes the weather with hacer: Hace sol, Hace frío, Hace calor. For cloudy or rainy skies it switches to estar: Está nublado. The seasons are la primavera, el verano, el otoño, el invierno — and they're handy for small talk: En verano hace calor.

examples.meaning: It's sunny.
It's very cold.
It's cloudy.
In winter it's cold.

concepts.commonError: Weather takes hace, not es: Hace frío, never Es frío.

concepts.title: Telling the time
concepts.explanation: Ask with ¿Qué hora es? One o'clock is special: Es la una. Every other hour uses son: Son las dos, Son las diez. Half past is y media, quarter past is y cuarto, and quarter to counts backwards: menos cuarto.

examples.meaning: What time is it?
It's one o'clock.
It's half past three.
It's quarter to two.

concepts.commonError: It's Es la una but Son las dos — the verb agrees with the hour.

concepts.title: Months and dates
concepts.explanation: The twelve months are masculine and always lowercase: enero, mayo, diciembre. Dates put the day first with el: el 3 de mayo, el 20 de diciembre. For birthdays, the pattern is Mi cumpleaños es el 5 de enero — or simply en junio for the month alone.

examples.meaning: Today is May 3rd.
My birthday is in June.

examples.target: La fiesta es el 20 de diciembre.
examples.meaning: The party is on December 20th.

concepts.commonError: Months are never capitalised in Spanish: en junio, not en Junio.

concepts.title: At the market
concepts.explanation: Quantities pair with de: un kilo de manzanas, una botella de agua, medio kilo de queso. To point at something near you, use este for masculine and esta for feminine: Este pan está fresco, Esta fruta es buena.

examples.meaning: A kilo of apples.
A bottle of water.
This bread is fresh.

examples.target: Medio kilo de queso, por favor.
examples.meaning: Half a kilo of cheese, please.

concepts.commonError: The quantity needs its de: un kilo de manzanas, never un kilo manzanas.

concepts.title: Free time and hobbies
concepts.explanation: Hobbies love the infinitive: Me gusta leer, Me encanta nadar. With an infinitive, gustar always stays singular — the action counts as one thing. For stronger feelings there's encantar: Me encanta el cine. And sports take jugar: Juego al fútbol, with al fusing a + el.

examples.meaning: I like reading.
I love swimming.
I play soccer.
Do you like the movies?

concepts.commonError: With two infinitives gustar still stays singular: Me gusta leer y nadar.

concepts.title: Health and the body
concepts.explanation: Pain in Spanish works like liking: Me duele la cabeza — the head hurts to me. One body part takes duele, several take duelen: Me duelen las manos. Note the article, not the possessive: la cabeza, never mi cabeza. For care, Voy al médico.

examples.meaning: My head hurts.
My hands hurt.
I have a fever.
I'm going to the doctor tomorrow.

concepts.commonError: Body parts take the article: Me duele la cabeza, not Me duele mi cabeza.

concepts.title: At the pharmacy
concepts.explanation: Necesito opens every request: Necesito estas pastillas. Ask the pharmacist with ¿Tiene algo para…?: ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de cabeza? Para marks purpose — for the pain — where por would mean because of it. Useful to hear: Es sin receta, no prescription needed.

examples.meaning: I need these pills.

examples.target: ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de cabeza?
examples.meaning: Do you have something for a headache?
It's without prescription.

concepts.commonError: Purpose takes para: algo para el dolor, never algo por el dolor.

concepts.title: Emergencies
concepts.explanation: ¡Socorro! is the cry for help; ¡Ayuda! works too. In a real emergency, use the formal command: ¡Llame a una ambulancia! Llame is the usted form — emergencies are no place for informality. Ask ¿Dónde está el hospital? or ¿Dónde hay un hospital?

examples.meaning: Help!

examples.target: Llame a una ambulancia, por favor.
examples.meaning: Call an ambulance, please.
Where is the hospital?
I need help.

concepts.commonError: Emergencies use the formal command: Llame, not the informal Llama.

concepts.title: Invitations
concepts.explanation: Te invito a… opens the invitation: Te invito a cenar. Ask ¿Quieres venir? or ¿Vienes a la fiesta? Accept warmly with ¡Claro que sí! Decline softly with Lo siento, no puedo — sorry, I can't — which keeps the door open.

examples.meaning: I invite you to dinner.
Do you want to come?
Of course, thank you!
I'm sorry, I can't.

concepts.commonError: Invitar takes a: Te invito a cenar, never Te invito cenar.

concepts.title: El pretérito: las formas
concepts.explanation: The pretérito reports finished actions. Habit first: anchor every past verb to a finished moment — ayer, anoche, el sábado. Pattern second: -ar endings -é/-aste/-ó, -er/-ir endings -í/-iste/-ió, and a small gang of irregulars (tuve, hice, dije, estuvo, fue) that ignore the pattern completely.

examples.meaning: Yesterday I worked until late.
We ate paella on Sunday.
He was ill yesterday.
He told me no.

concepts.commonError: Present endings in a past story (*Hablo ayer) break the spell. Ayer forces the past: Ayer hablé. Watch the accent — hablo is I speak, hablé is I spoke.

concepts.title: El imperfecto: el pasado en curso
concepts.explanation: The imperfecto describes what was ongoing or habitual: settings (era de noche), habits (jugaba cada día), background (mientras cenábamos). Habit first: if you can add 'used to' or 'was -ing' in English, reach for the imperfecto. Pattern second: -aba for -ar, -ía for -er/-ir; only era, iba, veía break it.

examples.meaning: As a kid I used to play football.
It was a calm afternoon.

examples.target: Había mucha gente en la plaza.
examples.meaning: There were a lot of people in the square.
While we were having dinner, the phone rang.

concepts.commonError: Don't use the pretérito for background: *Fue una tarde tranquila sounds like the calm ended on schedule. A scene that simply was → Era una tarde tranquila.

concepts.title: Elegir el pasado: evento o fondo
concepts.explanation: Two pasts, two jobs. Pretérito = what happened, finished and counted (llovió, sonó, vi). Imperfecto = what was happening, the background film (llovía, dormía, jugaba). Habit first: ask 'did it finish, or was it ongoing?' Pattern second: finished-time words (ayer, una vez, de repente) → pretérito; habitual words (siempre, todos los días, de niño, mientras) → imperfecto.

examples.meaning: Last week it rained a lot.
As a child it used to rain a lot.
While I was sleeping, the phone rang.

examples.target: Una vez vi una película genial.
examples.meaning: Once I saw a great movie.

concepts.commonError: Don't let a finished time word wear the imperfecto: *La semana pasada llovía treats one finished week as an endless habit. Finished frame → llovió.

concepts.title: Narrar el fin de semana
concepts.explanation: A weekend story runs on two rails: time anchors (el sábado, por la mañana, el domingo) and finished verbs (fui, vimos, descansé). Habit first: say when, then say what — the anchor licenses the past tense. Pattern second: primero → después → por último chains the events in order.

examples.meaning: On Saturday I went to the market.

examples.target: Por la tarde vimos una película.
examples.meaning: In the afternoon we watched a movie.
On Sunday I rested at home.

examples.target: Primero desayuné, después salí a correr.
examples.meaning: First I had breakfast, then I went out for a run.

concepts.commonError: Don't narrate finished events in the present: *El sábado voy al cine describes a habit, not last Saturday. It happened → El sábado fui al cine.

concepts.title: El futuro simple: las formas
concepts.explanation: The futuro simple predicts and promises. Habit first: attach it to tomorrow-words — mañana, el lunes, la próxima semana. Pattern second: whole infinitive + é/ás/á/emos/án, identical for -ar, -er and -ir. Six stems rebel: tener→tendr-, poder→podr-, hacer→har-, decir→dir-, venir→vendr-, salir→saldr-.

examples.meaning: Tomorrow I will speak with him.
We will eat at two.
I will have time on Friday.
I will do the homework tonight.

concepts.commonError: Don't conjugate first and then add: *hablo + é is wrong. The future keeps the whole infinitive — hablar + é = hablaré.

concepts.title: Para qué sirve el futuro
concepts.explanation: Three habits, one tense. Promise: te llamaré, vendré — the speaker commits. Prediction: lloverá, será — the speaker forecasts, often boosted by creo que/probablemente/seguro. Supposition: estará en casa — the future guesses about the present. Habit first: hear the intention behind the verb, not just the time.

examples.meaning: I will call you tonight.
Tomorrow it will rain.
He must be at home now.
He will probably come late.

concepts.commonError: Don't use the future for a plan you already decided and booked: Mañana *viajaré sounds like a forecast. Decided plan → Voy a viajar. The future predicts; ir a executes.

concepts.title: Ir a + infinitivo: los planes
concepts.explanation: Ir a + infinitive is the near future of decided plans: voy a, vas a, va a, vamos a. Habit first: if you could add 'I've decided' in English, use ir a. Pattern second: conjugate ir, add a, keep the second verb untouched. Querer names the wish behind the plan: Quiero viajar.

examples.meaning: I am going to study medicine.
Are you going to come to the party?
We are going to buy a house.
I want to learn Italian.

concepts.commonError: Don't stack them: *Voy a querer is clumsy. A wish is Quiero; a decided plan is Voy a + verb. One job per construction.

concepts.title: El condicional: would
concepts.explanation: The condicional imagines: wishes (me gustaría), advice (deberías), polite requests (¿podrías?). Habit first: if English says would/could/should, reach for the condicional. Pattern second: infinitive + ía/ías/ía/íamos/ían — the future's endings with the stress moved. Same six rebel stems as the future: podría, tendría, haría, diría, vendría, saldría.

examples.meaning: I would like to travel to Japan.
Could you help me?
You should rest more.
It would be great to see you.

concepts.commonError: Don't use the future for would: *Me gustará viajar means I will like traveling — a prediction, not a wish. Would needs the -ía ending: Me gustaría.

concepts.title: Pedir con cortesía
concepts.explanation: To ask like a local, borrow would: Me gustaría + noun/infinitive, Quisiera + noun/infinitive. Habit first: in shops, restaurants and hotels, start every request with one of them — never the bare imperative. Pattern second: Me gustaría una mesa; Quisiera la cuenta; ¿Sería tan amable de ayudarme?

examples.target: Me gustaría una mesa para dos.
examples.meaning: I would like a table for two.
I would like to speak with the manager.
Would you be so kind as to help me?
I would love to come back.

concepts.commonError: Don't order with the imperative among strangers: *Dame la cuenta barks. Quisiera la cuenta, por favor asks — and gets a smile.

concepts.title: El subjuntivo tras quiero que
concepts.explanation: Two subjects, one wish → the second verb goes subjunctive: Quiero (I) que vengas (you). Habit first: hear quiero que / necesito que / es importante que as an alarm bell — the next verb changes. Pattern second: yo-present minus -o plus opposite endings (hable, coma, viva); key forms: vengas, hables, quiera, pueda, sea, digas.

examples.target: Quiero que vengas a la fiesta.
examples.meaning: I want you to come to the party.
I need you to help me.
It's important that you study.
I want you to speak more slowly.

concepts.commonError: Don't keep the indicative after que: *Quiero que vienes is the classic mistake. One wisher, one other person → the second verb must be subjunctive: Quiero que vengas.

concepts.title: Oraciones de relativo
concepts.explanation: Relative words replace a whole second sentence. Habit first: need to add information about a noun? Reach for que — it covers things, people (without preposition) and ideas. Pattern second: person + preposition → quien/quienes (con quien hablé); place → donde (donde vivo); the-one-that → el que; what/that-which → lo que.

examples.target: El libro que leí es genial.
examples.meaning: The book (that) I read is great.

examples.target: La persona con quien hablé fue amable.
examples.meaning: The person with whom I spoke was kind.

examples.target: La ciudad donde vivo es pequeña.
examples.meaning: The city where I live is small.
What you say is true.

concepts.commonError: Don't use que for people after a preposition: *la persona con que hablé is wrong. People + preposition → con quien.

concepts.title: Comparar: más, menos, tan… como
concepts.explanation: Habit first: comparing two things? más/menos + adjective + que. Saying they're equal? tan + adjective + como. Pattern second: bueno→mejor, malo→peor, grande→mayor, pequeño→menor — the four rebels replace the whole formula. Before a number, que becomes de: más de tres.

examples.target: Madrid es más grande que Sevilla.
examples.meaning: Madrid is bigger than Seville.

examples.target: Mi piso es menos caro que el tuyo.
examples.meaning: My flat is less expensive than yours.

examples.target: Es tan alto como su hermano.
examples.meaning: He is as tall as his brother.
This restaurant is the best.

concepts.commonError: Don't stack comparisons: *más mejor is wrong — mejor already contains the 'more'. One comparison per sentence.

concepts.title: Pronombres de objeto
concepts.explanation: Habit first: about to repeat a noun? Replace it. Lo/la = him/her/it (direct: what you see, buy, give). Le/les = to him/her/them (indirect: who receives). Pattern second: pronouns go before the conjugated verb (Lo veo, Le di); two pronouns together go indirect-then-direct, and le+lo melts into se lo.

examples.meaning: I see him/it every day.
I bought it (feminine) yesterday.

examples.target: Le di el libro a María.
examples.meaning: I gave the book to María.
He gave it to me yesterday.

concepts.commonError: Don't keep both: *Le lo di is wrong — le + lo melts into se lo: Se lo di. Se is the diplomat that prevents le-lo collisions.

concepts.title: Por o para
concepts.explanation: Habit first: explaining a cause or moving through space → por. Naming a goal, a recipient or a deadline → para. Pattern second: por = because of / through / in exchange for (por eso, por aquí, gracias por); para = in order to / for (a recipient) / by (a deadline) (para aprender, para ti, para mañana).

examples.meaning: Come this way, please.
It's for you.
I study (in order) to learn.
Thanks for your help.

concepts.commonError: Don't swap them: *Estudio por aprender is wrong — purpose is para: Estudio para aprender. Por explains what already happened; para points at what's next.

concepts.title: El superlativo
concepts.explanation: Habit first: crowning one above all? el/la/los/las + más + adjective + de: el más alto de la clase. Going extreme? -ísimo on the adjective: buenísimo, rapidísimo. Pattern second: the article must match the noun (los más amables); -ísimo drops the adjective's final vowel (bueno→buenísimo, grande→grandísima).

examples.target: Es el más alto de la clase.
examples.meaning: He is the tallest in the class.
She is a really good person.
I have an interview tomorrow.
My schedule is flexible.

concepts.commonError: Don't forget the article: *Es más alto de la clase is just a comparison with a missing rival. The crown needs el: Es el más alto de la clase.

concepts.title: Misión: en el hotel
concepts.explanation: Checking in is a script: greet, confirm the reservation, get the key, ask about breakfast. When something breaks, the magic frame is No hay… — No hay agua caliente, no hay toallas. Report, don't apologize: name what's missing and the desk will fix it.

examples.target: Tengo una reserva a nombre de García.
examples.meaning: I have a reservation under García.

examples.target: Aquí tiene la llave de su habitación.
examples.meaning: Here is your room key.
What time is breakfast?
There is no hot water.

concepts.commonError: Don't say *Tengo una reservación — the word is reserva. And it's la llave, feminine even though it ends in -e.

concepts.title: Hablar de tecnología
concepts.explanation: Habit first: tech problems are reported with estar + adjective (está rota, no funciona) and fixed with regular verbs (enciende, descarga, envía). Pattern second: most tech nouns are masculine (el móvil, el ordenador, el wifi); asking for the password is always ¿Cuál es la contraseña de…? with del before masculine nouns.

examples.meaning: What is the wifi password?
I'll send you the document now.
The screen is broken.
Download the app.

concepts.commonError: Don't translate word by word: *la contraseña de el wifi is wrong. De + el always contracts: la contraseña del wifi.

concepts.title: Narrar en pasado
concepts.explanation: A story in Spanish runs on two past tenses working together. The pretérito reports what happened — finished events like fui, perdió, llegamos. The imperfecto paints the scene around those events: the time, the crowd, the weather (eran las seis, había mucha gente). Time markers join the beats in order: primero, luego, después and al final.

examples.target: Hubo un problema en las vías.
examples.meaning: There was a problem on the tracks (a finished event).

examples.target: Había mucha gente en la estación.
examples.meaning: There were lots of people at the station (a scene).

concepts.commonError: Using the pretérito for the scene: describe the background with había, not hubo.

concepts.title: La noticia de viajes
concepts.explanation: A news report about travel keeps three habits. The pretérito reports what already happened (canceló, esperaron). The conditional says what would happen next (reprogramaría, sería, habría). The rebooking words carry the story: the retraso, the cancelación, the new horario, reprogramar.

examples.target: La compañía dijo que reprogramaría los vuelos.
examples.meaning: The airline said it would rebook the flights.
It might be possible to leave on Sunday.

concepts.commonError: Using the future instead of the conditional for what the company announced it would do: the report softens it with -ría.

concepts.title: En el aeropuerto
concepts.explanation: At an airport or station, the numbers and times do the work: falta una hora (there is an hour to go), el embarque es a las siete y cuarto, la puerta doce. When an announcement passes you by, interrupt politely with Perdone… and ask for a repeat: ¿Puede repetir, por favor?

examples.target: Falta una hora para el vuelo.
examples.meaning: There is still an hour before the flight.
Excuse me, could you repeat that, please?

concepts.commonError: Interrupting without the polite opener: Perdone… before the question keeps the exchange courteous.

concepts.title: Cambiar el viaje con cortesía
concepts.explanation: Soft requests at a travel counter run on the conditional and the polite imperfect: me gustaría, podría, quería, quisiera — all courteous, none a demand. Add porque plus a full sentence to give the reason: lo cambio porque tengo una reunión.

examples.meaning: I would like to change my flight.

examples.target: Quería preguntar por el vuelo de mañana.
examples.meaning: I wanted to ask about tomorrow's flight.

concepts.commonError: Dropping the polite frame and using the direct present (quiero) with an agent: the counter register softens with the conditional.

concepts.title: Contar el viaje por escrito
concepts.explanation: A written story needs the same skeleton as the spoken one: first, then, after, in the end — primero, luego, después, al final — plus a reason when it matters, introduced by porque. Short, connected sentences with a clear ending read best.

examples.target: Primero perdimos el tren de las nueve.
examples.meaning: First we missed the nine o'clock train.

examples.target: Llegamos tarde porque el tráfico era horrible.
examples.meaning: We arrived late because the traffic was terrible.

concepts.commonError: Piling events without markers: a porque or a time marker on each sentence keeps the reader oriented.

concepts.title: Reclamar en el mostrador
concepts.explanation: A polite complaint at a service desk opens with quisiera (or quería) plus an infinitive: Quisiera reclamar una indemnización. To report what you were told, Spanish uses dijo que or me dijeron que, and the tense after que can stay close to the original words: me dijeron que el vuelo salía a las nueve.

examples.meaning: I would like to claim compensation.

examples.target: Me dijeron que el vuelo salía a las nueve.
examples.meaning: They told me the flight left at nine.

concepts.commonError: Opening with a blunt quiero at the desk: quisiera or quería keeps the complaint courteous.

concepts.title: Hablar de planes
concepts.explanation: Spanish splits plans three ways. Decided plans you have already arranged use ir a + infinitive: El año que viene voy a trabajar en una oficina. Fixed schedules — timetables, classes, calendars — use the present: El curso empieza en septiembre. Predictions and promises use the future simple: Trabajaré en el extranjero algún día. Porque joins a plan to its reason: voy a estudiar enfermería porque quiero trabajar en un hospital.

examples.target: El año que viene voy a estudiar enfermería.
examples.meaning: Next year I'm going to study nursing (a decided plan).

examples.target: Las clases de inglés empiezan a las nueve.
examples.meaning: The English classes start at nine (a fixed schedule).
Afterwards I'll work in a hospital (a prediction).

concepts.commonError: Using the future simple for a plan you have already arranged: decided plans take ir a — voy a estudiar, not estudiaré.

concepts.title: La llamada de la oferta
concepts.explanation: A job-offer call runs on a few spoken routines. Turn-taking openers keep the call alive: a ver, ¿me oyes? Offers come in the conditional: podría empezar el lunes. Salaries and hours are spoken numbers: unos mil ochocientos euros. And estar de + activity names temporary work: estoy de becaria en la agencia.

examples.meaning: Hello, can you hear me well?
I could start on Monday.

examples.target: Estoy de becaria en una agencia.
examples.meaning: I'm working as an intern at an agency.

concepts.commonError: Using ser for temporary work: estar de names the temporary role — estoy de becaria, not soy becaria.

concepts.title: Leer una entrevista
concepts.explanation: An interview write-up compares and evaluates. Más que and menos que weigh two things (este puesto es más estable que el otro), tan… como levels them, and el más or -ísimo crowns the best. The relative que links people and things (la empresa que me contrató); quien stays personal (el jefe con quien hablé). Porque justifies the choice.

examples.target: La editorial es más conocida que la agencia.
examples.meaning: The publishing house is more well-known than the agency.

examples.target: La agencia es tan joven como flexible.
examples.meaning: The agency is as young as it is flexible.

examples.target: Es la mejor opción para empezar.
examples.meaning: It is the best option to start with.

concepts.commonError: Using quien for things: the relative que covers people and things — la oficina que visité, not la oficina quien visité.

concepts.title: Elegir entre dos ofertas
concepts.explanation: Choosing between two offers uses comparatives (el puesto de la editorial es más seguro que el de la cafetería), soft advice with deberías (deberías pedir más información) and reasons with porque. Deberías advises; debes commands.

examples.target: La agencia es más pequeña que la editorial.
examples.meaning: The agency is smaller than the publishing house.
You should compare the two offers.

examples.target: Prefiero la agencia porque el equipo es pequeño.
examples.meaning: I prefer the agency because the team is small.

concepts.commonError: Pushing with debes when advice is expected: deberías keeps the advice soft.

concepts.title: Escribir tu plan
concepts.explanation: A written plan hangs together: sequence markers (primero, luego, al final) order the steps, ir a or the future simple carry the plan forward, and at least one porque reason explains why.

examples.target: Primero voy a terminar el curso.
examples.meaning: First I'm going to finish the course.
Afterwards I'll apply for the scholarship.

examples.target: Al final buscaré trabajo porque necesito experiencia.
examples.meaning: In the end I'll look for work because I need experience.

concepts.commonError: Listing steps without a porque reason: a written plan explains at least one of its choices.

concepts.title: La entrevista de trabajo
concepts.explanation: A job interview opens with self-presentation: me llamo…, soy de…, llevo… . Polite requests use quisiera or podría. Espero que takes the subjunctive: espero que el equipo sea acogedor.

examples.target: Me llamo Lucía y soy de Zaragoza.
examples.meaning: My name is Lucía and I'm from Zaragoza.

examples.target: Llevo dos años de becaria en una revista.
examples.meaning: I've been an intern at a magazine for two years.

examples.target: Espero que el equipo sea acogedor.
examples.meaning: I hope the team is welcoming.

concepts.commonError: Saying espero que es instead of espero que sea: the hope trigger takes the subjunctive.

concepts.title: Gustar y porque
concepts.explanation: Preferences ride on gustar-type verbs: the thing liked agrees with the verb and the person appears as the dative (me gusta el cine, me gustan las películas). A preference earns a reason with porque plus a full sentence (lo prefiero porque está tranquilo), and porque — one word, no accent — is the reason; the question carries the accent and splits into two words: ¿por qué?

examples.target: Me gusta el cine porque las historias me emocionan.
examples.meaning: I like the cinema because the stories move me.

examples.target: Me gustan las películas de aventuras.
examples.meaning: I like adventure films.

examples.target: ¿Por qué prefieres el museo? — Porque está tranquilo.
examples.meaning: Why do you prefer the museum? — Because it is quiet.
I'm not coming because of work (por + noun).

concepts.commonError: Writing the reason with an accent: porque is one word without a tilde, por qué is the question.

concepts.title: La llamada del cumpleaños
concepts.explanation: A planning call runs on a few spoken frames. ¿Te apetece…? proposes the plan, claro que sí accepts it, lo siento, no puedo declines it. The plan itself moves with ir a (vamos a celebrar) and quedamos en + place fixes where; porque states the reason.

examples.target: ¿Te apetece venir a la fiesta el sábado?
examples.meaning: Do you fancy coming to the party on Saturday?
Of course. Where shall we meet?

examples.target: Quedamos en la plaza a las ocho.
examples.meaning: We'll meet at the square at eight.

examples.target: Vamos a celebrarlo con una cena.
examples.meaning: We're going to celebrate it with a dinner.

concepts.commonError: Declining without a courtesy: lo siento, no puedo keeps the decline friendly.

concepts.title: El aniversario
concepts.explanation: A group plan in writing mixes three moves: the conditional invitation (¿te gustaría organizar una cena?), purpose with para + infinitive (para celebrarlo, para regalar), and reasons with porque. Por + noun names the occasion (por su aniversario); para names the aim.

examples.meaning: Would you like to organise a dinner?
We are buying flowers to give as a gift.

examples.target: Celebramos la cena por su aniversario.
examples.meaning: We hold the dinner for their anniversary.

examples.target: La pareja prefiere casa porque es tranquilo.
examples.meaning: The couple prefers home because it is calm.

concepts.commonError: Swapping por and para with nouns: por names the cause or occasion, para names the aim — por su aniversario, para celebrarlo.

concepts.title: Quedar para la fiesta
concepts.explanation: Agreeing a plan runs on three frames: vamos a + infinitive states what you will do, quedamos en + place fixes where, and ¿qué te parece? asks the other's view. Accept with claro que sí; decline with lo siento, no puedo — then propose again.

examples.meaning: We're going to celebrate it on Saturday.

examples.target: ¿Quedamos en la plaza a las ocho?
examples.meaning: Shall we meet at the square at eight?

examples.target: ¿Qué te parece si vamos al cine?
examples.meaning: What do you think about going to the cinema?

concepts.commonError: Proposing without asking: ¿qué te parece? keeps the plan a shared decision.

concepts.title: Justificar una decisión
concepts.explanation: A written decision reads clearly when it opens with the choice (me gustaría, prefiero), gives a porque reason, and closes with the agreed plan (quedamos en, vamos a). Porque — one word, no accent — states the reason; por qué asks.

examples.target: Prefiero el parque porque es tranquilo.
examples.meaning: I prefer the park because it is quiet.
I would like to celebrate it at home.

examples.target: Quedamos en la fuente a las seis.
examples.meaning: We'll meet at the fountain at six.
Why don't we celebrate on Saturday?

concepts.commonError: Deciding without a reason: a written decision explains at least one porque choice.

concepts.title: El regalo del grupo
concepts.explanation: A group gift needs two prepositions and one clitic rule. Por names the occasion (por su cumpleaños); para names the aim (para regalar). With two object pronouns Spanish swaps le lo for se lo: se lo compro esta tarde (I'll buy it for him this afternoon); te lo doy el sábado (I'll give it to you on Saturday).

examples.target: Compramos un libro por su cumpleaños.
examples.meaning: We are buying a book for his birthday (the occasion).

examples.target: El libro es para regalar a Andrés.
examples.meaning: The book is to give to Andrés.
I'll buy it for him this afternoon.

examples.target: Te lo llevo a la fiesta.
examples.meaning: I'll bring it to you at the party.

concepts.commonError: Saying le lo: with two pronouns the dative le becomes se — se lo compro, not le lo compro.

concepts.title: Conectar la narración
concepts.explanation: A connected story links its beats. Mientras + imperfecto sets the background: mientras esperaba, leía el periódico. Cuando + pretérito lands the event: cuando llegó el tren, salimos. Pero and aunque add the contrast: al final llegamos tarde, pero todo salió bien. The sequence markers — primero, luego, después, al final — order the tale.

examples.meaning: While I waited, I was reading the paper.

examples.target: Cuando llegó el tren, salimos corriendo.
examples.meaning: When the train arrived, we ran out.

examples.target: Primero compré los billetes; luego busqué el andén.
examples.meaning: First I bought the tickets; then I looked for the platform.

examples.target: Al final llegamos tarde, pero todo salió bien.
examples.meaning: In the end we arrived late, but everything turned out well.
Although it was raining, we walked.

concepts.commonError: A story of only pretérito sentences, with no background (mientras + imperfecto) and no contrast (pero, aunque), reads flat.

concepts.title: Seguir una anécdota hablada
concepts.explanation: Spoken narration runs on small markers: pues starts the tale, entonces steps it forward, and al final resultó que delivers the twist. The tenses switch as the story does: mientras + imperfecto for the scene, pretérito for what happened.

examples.target: Pues fui al mercado con mi hermana.
examples.meaning: Well, I went to the market with my sister.

examples.target: Entonces me acordé de la chaqueta.
examples.meaning: Then I remembered the jacket.

examples.target: Al final resultó que estaban en el bolsillo.
examples.meaning: In the end it turned out they were in the pocket.
That's intense! And then?

concepts.commonError: Hearing only the verbs and missing the markers: pues, entonces and al final resultó que are the signposts that keep a spoken tale on track.

concepts.title: Un mensaje que se cruza
concepts.explanation: In a story about a message gone wrong, reported frames carry the plot: me dijo que / le dije que + a past clause. Mientras paints the background, porque gives the reason, and the twist lands when the message does not match the plan.

examples.target: Me dijo que el tren salía a las siete.
examples.meaning: He told me the train left at seven.

examples.target: Le dije que esperaría en el andén.
examples.meaning: I told him I would wait on the platform.
While we waited, it was raining.

examples.target: No vino porque leyó mal el mensaje.
examples.meaning: He did not come because he misread the message.

concepts.commonError: Dropping the que of the report: me dijo el tren salía — the reported clause keeps its que.

concepts.title: Reaccionar a una historia
concepts.explanation: A good listener keeps the story going: ¿en serio? asks for confirmation, ¡qué fuerte! shares the shock, ¿y luego? and ¿y qué hiciste? pull the next beat, and porque or aunque in the reply keeps the thread.

examples.target: ¿En serio? No me lo puedo creer.
examples.meaning: Really? I can't believe it.
That's intense! And what happened next?
And what did you do when you saw it?

examples.target: Fui a casa, aunque estaba cansado.
examples.meaning: I went home, although I was tired.

concepts.commonError: Answering yes or no to a story: the listener keeps the tale moving with ¿y luego? and ¿y qué hiciste?, not with sí or no alone.

concepts.title: Un relato en pocas líneas
concepts.explanation: A written account opens with primero, moves with luego or después, and closes with al final — plus one porque or pero clause. The porque reason explains, the pero contrast turns the tale.

examples.meaning: First I went to the bakery.
Then I walked back home.

examples.target: Al final llegué tarde, porque el autobús no pasaba.
examples.meaning: In the end I was late, because the bus was not coming.

examples.target: Pero la tarde fue buena igualmente.
examples.meaning: But the afternoon was good all the same.

concepts.commonError: A paragraph of unlinked sentences: the account needs its markers — primero, luego, al final — and one porque or pero clause.

concepts.title: Contar tu anécdota
concepts.explanation: Retelling your anecdote to a new listener uses the same skeleton: tuve que or decidí for the event, al final resultó que for the twist, and a reaction closer for the listener.

examples.target: Tuve que volver a casa andando.
examples.meaning: I had to walk back home.
I decided to wait on the platform.

examples.target: Al final resultó que era otro andén.
examples.meaning: In the end it turned out it was another platform.
Lucky that everything turned out well!

concepts.commonError: Ending the tale with no closer: after the twist, the retell needs a reaction — ¡qué suerte! or ¡menudo susto! — for the listener.

concepts.title: Conectar causa y consecuencia
concepts.explanation: Consequence connectors link a cause to what follows from it: por eso, así que and entonces all sit at the start of the consequence clause. Porque looks backwards to the reason; por eso, así que and entonces look forwards to what happens because of it. Cause first, then the connector, then the consequence: Llueve, por eso llevo el paraguas.

examples.target: Llueve, por eso llevo el paraguas.
examples.meaning: It's raining, that's why I take the umbrella.

examples.target: Perdí el tren, así que llegué tarde.
examples.meaning: I missed the train, so I arrived late.

examples.target: No había autobuses, entonces fuimos andando.
examples.meaning: There were no buses, so we walked.

concepts.commonError: Using porque for the consequence too: porque gives the cause - the consequence takes por eso, así que or entonces.

concepts.title: Planes y su desenlace
concepts.explanation: A changed-plan account runs on outcome frames: pensaba que + a past clause sets the original idea, al final marks the turn, and salió bien or salió mal closes the account. Because and consequence both belong in the same text: porque gives the reason for the change, por eso names what followed from it. These frames are a common way speakers and writers tell a before-and-after story - a convention of the telling, not a fixed rule.

examples.target: Pensaba que el tren salía a las siete.
examples.meaning: I thought the train left at seven.
In the end we changed our plans.

examples.target: Llovía, por eso lo dejamos para otro día.
examples.meaning: It was raining, that's why we put it off for another day.

concepts.commonError: Telling the change without the frame: the before-and-after needs its markers - pensaba que… sets the original plan, al final turns it, salió bien or salió mal closes it.

concepts.title: Si pasa esto, entonces…
concepts.explanation: An open conditional sets a real possibility in the present and names what follows: si + present in the condition clause, then the consequence with the future or ir a. Si llueve, nos quedaremos en casa. Si hace bueno, vamos a ir al parque. The question frame ¿y si…? proposes the possibility itself: ¿y si llueve? - what if it rains?

examples.target: Si llueve, nos quedaremos en casa.
examples.meaning: If it rains, we'll stay at home.

examples.target: Si hace bueno, vamos a ir al parque.
examples.meaning: If the weather's nice, we're going to the park.
What if it rains?

concepts.commonError: A future tense inside the condition: si lloverá - Spanish keeps the present after si (si llueve) and puts the future or ir a in the consequence.

concepts.title: Negociar un cambio de plan
concepts.explanation: A change-of-plan negotiation uses soft frames: ¿qué tal si…? proposes the new idea, mejor… prefers it, nos quedamos en… fixes the fallback, and lo dejamos para otro día delays it. The reason travels with the change: porque gives it, por eso or así que carry the consequence of the decision. These frames are a common, friendly way to renegotiate - a convention of informal chat, not a fixed rule.

examples.meaning: How about we go to the cinema?
Better we stay at home.
We'll leave it for another day.

concepts.commonError: Announcing the change like an order: the friendly negotiation proposes (¿qué tal si…?), prefers (mejor…), and delays (lo dejamos para otro día) instead of commanding.

concepts.title: El plan por escrito y su consecuencia
concepts.explanation: A short written plan runs on sequence and consequence: open with the plan (voy a + the infinitive or a future form), move with luego or después, and link the likely result with porque (the reason) or por eso (the consequence). Two to four connected sentences with one clear link read best.

examples.target: Voy a madrugar, por eso llegaré a tiempo.
examples.meaning: I'll get up early, that's why I'll be on time.

examples.target: Salgo con tiempo porque odio las prisas.
examples.meaning: I leave with time to spare because I hate rushing.

examples.target: Primero preparo la mochila; luego salgo.
examples.meaning: First I pack my bag; then I leave.

concepts.commonError: Writing the plan without its consequence: one porque (reason) or por eso (result) link turns a list of plans into a connected short text.

concepts.title: El plan al aire libre
concepts.explanation: An outdoor plan travels with its weather clause: the plan itself (vamos a or a future form), the backstop (¿y si llueve? - what if it rains?), and the decision with its consequence (por eso, así que). Polite re-planning softens the change: podríamos + the infinitive proposes gently, se podría names the option - a common, friendly way to keep the plan open.

examples.target: Vamos a hacer un picnic en el parque.
examples.meaning: We're going to have a picnic in the park.
What if it rains? Then the café.

examples.target: Podríamos dejar el picnic para el domingo.
examples.meaning: We could leave the picnic for Sunday.

concepts.commonError: Planning outdoors with no backstop: an outdoor plan keeps its second plan - ¿y si llueve? and the consequence with por eso or así que.

concepts.title: Dar una opinión
concepts.explanation: An opinion starts with a frame: creo que, pienso que or me parece que, followed by a normal indicative verb. The reason arrives with porque. To disagree, the trigger no creo que moves the verb after it into a fixed subjunctive form: no creo que sea una buena idea. The frame carries the disagreement; the phrase after it is a form to recognise.

examples.target: Creo que esta película es muy buena.
examples.meaning: I think this film is very good.

examples.target: Me parece que el restaurante nuevo está caro.
examples.meaning: It seems to me the new restaurant is expensive.

examples.target: Pienso que llegaremos a tiempo, porque salimos pronto.
examples.meaning: I think we will arrive on time, because we are leaving early.

examples.target: No creo que sea mala idea probarlo.
examples.meaning: I do not think it is a bad idea to try it.

concepts.commonError: Opinions without their frame: creo que, pienso que and me parece que are the signals that tell the listener an opinion is coming — a bare verb can read as a statement of fact.

concepts.title: Seguir una discusión de opiniones
concepts.explanation: A spoken discussion keeps its opinions soft: creo que and me parece que open the views, and the disagreement rides small moves — bueno, sí, pero…, a ver, ¿tú qué crees? — that keep the talk friendly. The porque reason keeps every opinion grounded.

examples.target: Bueno, sí, tiene su encanto, pero yo casi no voy.
examples.meaning: Well, yes, it has its charm, but I hardly ever go.

examples.target: A ver, ¿y si preguntamos a los vecinos?
examples.meaning: Let's see, what if we ask the neighbours?
What do you think? Do we close it or not?

examples.target: Me parece que el barrio lo necesita.
examples.meaning: It seems to me the neighbourhood needs it.

concepts.commonError: Hearing only the opinions and missing the softeners: bueno and a ver mark the polite turn, not the verdict.

concepts.title: Estar de acuerdo y discrepar con cortesía
concepts.explanation: Agreement comes in two sizes: de acuerdo nods alone, and estoy de acuerdo carries the verb. The polite no is no estoy seguro, and every move lands better with the porque reason attached: estoy de acuerdo, porque así ganamos tiempo. Tienes razón hands the point over.

examples.target: Tienes razón: la idea es buena.
examples.meaning: You're right: the idea is good.
I agree with you.
Agreed, let's do it.

examples.target: No estoy seguro de que sea tan fácil.
examples.meaning: I'm not sure it's that easy.

examples.target: Estoy de acuerdo, porque así ganamos tiempo.
examples.meaning: I agree, because that way we save time.

concepts.commonError: Agreeing or disagreeing without the frame: de acuerdo nods alone, estoy de acuerdo carries the verb, and the porque reason keeps the exchange on the topic.

concepts.title: Opinar en un intercambio
concepts.explanation: A discussion of a choice keeps the frames soft: creo que and me parece que give the view and porque the reason, while no estoy seguro softens the no. When the thread crosses, the repair is small: perdona, que no te he oído bien. The fixed form no creo que + the subjunctive stays a phrase to recognise, not to build.

examples.target: Creo que el regalo de todos es mejor, porque así es más especial.
examples.meaning: I think a present from everyone is better, because that makes it more special.

examples.target: No estoy seguro de que le guste el libro.
examples.meaning: I'm not sure she'll like the book.

examples.target: Perdona, que no te he oído bien: ¿decías un libro?
examples.meaning: Sorry, I didn't hear you well: were you saying a book?

examples.target: No creo que sea mala idea preguntarle.
examples.meaning: I don't think it's a bad idea to ask her.

concepts.commonError: Answering an opinion with a bare no: the polite no keeps a frame (no estoy seguro, no creo que…, no pienso igual) plus the porque reason.

concepts.title: Una opinión por escrito
concepts.explanation: A written opinion shows its order: the frame (creo que, me parece que or en mi opinión) opens, porque gives the reason, and además or por ejemplo adds the supporting detail. Written Spanish prefers the calmer frames — en mi opinión sits comfortably on paper, where chat shortens creo que to creo.

examples.target: En mi opinión, el libro es estupendo.
examples.meaning: In my opinion, the book is excellent.

examples.target: Creo que la película vale la pena, porque la historia engancha.
examples.meaning: I think the film is worth it, because the story grips you.
Also, the actors are great.

examples.target: Por ejemplo, yo la vi dos veces.
examples.meaning: For example, I saw it twice.

concepts.commonError: An opinion with no detail behind it: the porque reason and the además line are what make the written view worth reading.

concepts.title: Recomendar a un recién llegado
concepts.explanation: A recommendation is an opinion built for a new listener: the frame opens (me parece que, en mi opinión), porque gives the reason, además or por ejemplo the detail — and the para + purpose line says what it is for: es perfecto para una cena tranquila. The friendly closer (te lo recomiendo) hands it over.

examples.target: Me parece que el restaurante del puerto es genial.
examples.meaning: It seems to me the restaurant at the port is great.

examples.target: La comida es rica, porque todo es fresco.
examples.meaning: The food is delicious, because everything is fresh.

examples.target: Además, la terraza mira al mar.
examples.meaning: Also, the terrace looks out to sea.

examples.target: Es perfecto para una cena tranquila. Te lo recomiendo.
examples.meaning: It's perfect for a quiet dinner. I recommend it.

concepts.commonError: Recommending without the hook: the opinion frame, the porque reason and the para + purpose line are what make the newcomer say «¡pues voy!».

concepts.title: Describir un problema
concepts.explanation: A problem wears its frame: se ha estropeado names the recent breakdown, no funciona and funciona mal say how the thing behaves right now, and hay un problema con points straight at the thing. The se in se ha estropeado keeps the breakdown agentless: the machine broke; nobody did it. The polite ask rides its own frame: ¿me podría…? + the action.

examples.meaning: The washing machine has broken down.

examples.target: El wifi no funciona desde ayer.
examples.meaning: The wifi hasn't worked since yesterday.

examples.target: Hay un problema con la ducha: el agua sale fría.
examples.meaning: There's a problem with the shower: the water comes out cold.
The fridge works badly.

examples.target: ¿Me podría enviar a alguien esta semana?
examples.meaning: Could you send someone this week?

concepts.commonError: Reporting the problem without its frame: se ha estropeado, no funciona, hay un problema con and funciona mal are the signals that tell the listener what is wrong and whether it just happened or is still going on.

concepts.title: Seguir una llamada de servicio
concepts.explanation: A service call runs on spoken frames: llamo porque… opens with the reason, se ha estropeado and no funciona name the problem, and ¿me podría…? softens the ask. The past carries the story (dejó de centrifugar, empezó el lunes) and the present carries the state (no funciona, hace un ruido raro). The call walks problem → diagnosis → options → agreement.

examples.target: Llamo porque la lavadora se ha estropeado.
examples.meaning: I'm calling because the washing machine has broken down.
Could you confirm the time?
The noise started on Monday.
The home visit costs twenty euros.

examples.target: Quedamos en el jueves por la mañana.
examples.meaning: We settle on Thursday morning.

concepts.commonError: Hearing the diagnosis as the decision: the technician's first answer (suele ser la correa o la bomba) is a guess, not the fix — the agreement comes at the end, with the hour.

concepts.title: Pedir una solución
concepts.explanation: A solution gets built from three moves: the polite ask (¿me podría…? + the infinitive), the necessary step (hay que + the infinitive — a need that speaks for everyone), and the porque reason that makes the request honest: hay que arreglar el ascensor, porque no funciona bien. Hay que names the task, not the person: hay que cambiar la correa says the belt must change, whoever does it.

examples.target: ¿Me podría enviar a alguien esta semana?
examples.meaning: Could you send someone this week?
The lift has to be fixed.

examples.target: Hay que cambiar la correa de la lavadora.
examples.meaning: The washing machine belt has to be replaced.

examples.target: Hay que avisar al técnico esta tarde.
examples.meaning: The technician has to be notified this afternoon.

examples.target: Me vale si vienen el jueves por la mañana.
examples.meaning: It works for me if they come on Thursday morning.

concepts.commonError: Asking without the polite frame or the reason: ¿me podría…? opens the request, hay que states the necessary step, and porque keeps the ask grounded.

concepts.title: Negociar un arreglo
concepts.explanation: A fix gets settled inside the exchange: the polite ask opens, the alternative (¿qué tal si…?, mejor…) keeps the options open, and nos quedamos en… closes the deal. The porque reason keeps every offer honest, and when the thread crosses, the repair is small: perdona, ¿me repite la hora? The deal lands where both sides agree: nos quedamos en el jueves a las diez.

examples.target: ¿Qué tal si va el técnico el jueves?
examples.meaning: What if the technician goes on Thursday?

examples.target: Mejor por la mañana, porque estoy en casa.
examples.meaning: Better in the morning, because I'm at home.

examples.target: Nos quedamos en el jueves a las diez.
examples.meaning: We settle on Thursday at ten.
Sorry, can you repeat the time?

concepts.commonError: Talking past each other on the details: the hour and the day are the deal — confirm them with the small repair (perdona, ¿me repite la hora?) before the call ends.

concepts.title: Un informe por escrito
concepts.explanation: A written problem report shows its order: the problem opens (hay un problema con…, se ha estropeado…), porque gives the reason, and the consequence lands on por eso. The sequence markers (primero, luego, al final) keep the story easy to follow, and the polite ask closes the report: ¿me podría enviar a alguien esta semana?

examples.target: Hay un problema con la lavadora de casa.
examples.meaning: There's a problem with the washing machine at home.
First it stopped spinning.

examples.target: Luego empezó a hacer un ruido raro.
examples.meaning: Then it started making a strange noise.

examples.target: Por eso no puedo lavar la ropa aquí.
examples.meaning: That's why I can't wash my clothes here.

examples.target: ¿Me podría enviar a alguien esta semana?
examples.meaning: Could you send someone this week?

concepts.commonError: Reporting the problem without the consequence: the porque reason and the por eso line are what make the written report worth acting on.

concepts.title: Dejar el mensaje del arreglo
concepts.explanation: A fix relay speaks to a new listener with a clear order: llamo porque… opens with the reason, the frame names the problem (se ha estropeado), al final… carries the resolution (al final, nos quedamos en el jueves por la mañana), and the para + purpose line says what the visit is for: el técnico viene para arreglar la lavadora. The closing thanks hands the message over.

examples.target: Llamo porque la lavadora se ha estropeado.
examples.meaning: I'm calling because the washing machine has broken down.

examples.target: Al final, nos quedamos en el jueves por la mañana.
examples.meaning: In the end, we settled on Thursday morning.

examples.target: El técnico viene para arreglar la lavadora.
examples.meaning: The technician comes to fix the washing machine.
I'll be at home to let him in.
Thanks for everything.

concepts.commonError: Leaving the problem without the fix: the landlord needs the agreement (al final, nos quedamos en…) and the purpose (para arreglar), not just the breakdown.

concepts.title: Seguir el hilo
concepts.explanation: Signposts track a longer message: en primer lugar names the first point, por un lado… por otro lado holds two sides of one idea, luego steps forward, and al final lands the wrap-up. Es decir and o sea reformulate: they give the same idea a new shape instead of adding a new one. O sea is a reformulative connector documented in spoken register, so it belongs to the talk, not to the essay.

examples.target: En primer lugar, quiero hablar del horario.
examples.meaning: First of all, I want to talk about the timetable.

examples.target: Por un lado es caro, por otro lado es muy bueno.
examples.meaning: On the one hand it is expensive, on the other hand it is very good.
Then we move on to the second topic.
In the end, everything worked out well.

examples.target: O sea, que el plan sigue en pie.
examples.meaning: I mean, the plan is still on.

concepts.commonError: Hearing a reformulation as a new point: es decir and o sea do not add another idea, they re-state the one you just heard — count them as the same step of the thread, not a step forward.

concepts.title: Seguir una charla más larga
concepts.explanation: A longer talk holds its own thread: the claim opens it (bueno…), the example supports it, an aside may step away for a moment, and the wrap-up returns to the line (en fin, como decía…). The small spoken connectors are the handles: bueno opens, en fin gathers, and como decía… picks the thread back up after the detour. Listen for the reset phrases and the gist survives even the aside.

examples.target: Bueno, os cuento mi idea en dos minutos.
examples.meaning: Right, I'll tell you my idea in two minutes.

examples.target: En fin, que lo importante es empezar.
examples.meaning: Anyway, what matters is to start.

examples.target: Como decía, la huerta nos une.
examples.meaning: As I was saying, the garden brings us together.

examples.target: La huerta estará en el solar vacío.
examples.meaning: The vegetable garden will go on the empty plot.
You can sign up to help.

concepts.commonError: Losing the thread inside the aside: the detour (bueno, al principio… ) is not the talk — wait for the return (en fin, como decía…) and the wrap-up will name the point again.

concepts.title: Seguir una crónica
concepts.explanation: A longer text keeps its thread with organisation markers: según el autor hands the idea to its source, and la idea principal es… names the centre of the piece. Porque carries the reasons that hold the details together, and the pronouns look back — ella vuelve a abrir points at the library, su tejado at its roof — so each line ties to the one before and the reader keeps the gist without re-reading.

examples.target: Según el autor, la idea es clara.
examples.meaning: According to the author, the idea is clear.

examples.target: La idea principal es que la biblioteca reabre.
examples.meaning: The main idea is that the library is reopening.
The chronicle tells the story of the reopening.

examples.target: La biblioteca reabre porque terminaron las obras.
examples.meaning: The library reopens because the works have finished.
The roof had leaks.

concepts.commonError: Letting the pronouns drop the thread: when the text says ella or su, stop and ask who it points back to — the last named thing is usually the answer.

concepts.title: Aclarar una explicación
concepts.explanation: Repair keeps the thread alive in conversation: no te sigo says the thread is lost, ¿qué quieres decir? asks for the idea in fresh words, es decir que… re-states it, and perdona, ¿puedes repetir? buys a replay. The confirmation (ahora sí me queda claro) closes the repair — an exchange ends when both sides hold the same idea.

examples.meaning: Sorry, I'm not following you.
What do you mean by 'leaks'?

examples.target: Es decir que el agua pasaba por el tejado.
examples.meaning: That is to say, the water came through the roof.
Sorry, could you repeat the question?
Now it's clear to me.

concepts.commonError: Letting a lost thread go: no te sigo and ¿qué quieres decir? are normal turns, not failures — the repair is small and the exchange gets its thread back.

concepts.title: El resumen
concepts.explanation: A written summary hands the gist to a new reader: la idea principal es… names the centre, según + the source says where the idea came from, porque carries the reason, and además… and por ejemplo… add the details. Two to four connected sentences let someone who never saw the original follow the whole thread.

examples.target: La idea principal es que la biblioteca reabre.
examples.meaning: The main idea is that the library is reopening.

examples.target: Según la crónica, la idea es clara.
examples.meaning: According to the chronicle, the idea is clear.
Besides, they painted the rooms.

examples.target: Por ejemplo, la sala infantil tiene mesas nuevas.
examples.meaning: For example, the children's room has new tables.
The summary has four sentences.

concepts.commonError: Summarising in the order of the original piece: a summary reorganises — the main idea first, then the details, each tied to the source, so a new reader is not asked to retrace the whole text.

concepts.title: Pasar el hilo
concepts.explanation: A relay gives a new listener the whole thread: he escuchado / según + the source opens it, la idea principal es… names the centre, the signposts (por un lado… por otro lado…) carry the details, and the reaction closer (¡qué ganas de empezar!) hands over the feeling, not just the facts — a friend who missed the talk can still follow it.

examples.target: He escuchado una charla sobre la huerta.
examples.meaning: I listened to a talk about the vegetable garden.
The talk lasted ten minutes.

examples.target: O sea, que merece la pena.
examples.meaning: I mean, it is worth it.
I can't wait to start!
We are going to set up a vegetable garden.
The garden brings the neighbourhood together.

concepts.commonError: Relaying the facts without the thread: the friend needs the source, the main point, and the signposts that hold the details — and the reaction closer that says why you are telling them at all.

concepts.title: Ceder y contrastar
concepts.explanation: An argument moves in small beats: the stance frames creo que, en mi opinión and parece que hold the speaker's view; aunque concedes a point before the counter; pero joins the counter to the same sentence; and the adverbial connectors sin embargo, no obstante and en cambio open a contrasting sentence of their own. With a hypothetical situation, aunque takes the subjunctive: aunque lloviera, saldríamos igualmente. With a factual one, the indicative sounds neutral: aunque llueve, salimos igual.

examples.target: Creo que el barrio gana con la calle peatonal.
examples.meaning: I think the neighbourhood gains from the pedestrian street.

examples.target: Aunque el piso es pequeño, la luz lo compensa.
examples.meaning: Even though the flat is small, the light makes up for it.
Even if it rained, we would still go out.

examples.target: Sin embargo, el comercio no va a cerrar.
examples.meaning: However, the shops are not going to close.

examples.target: En cambio, la plaza se llenó de terrazas.
examples.meaning: By contrast, the square filled up with terraces.

concepts.commonError: Conceding as if it were agreeing: aunque does not change your position — it gives the other side a point before your counter. And aunque with a hypothetical stays in the subjunctive: aunque lloviera, not aunque lloverá.

concepts.title: Seguir un debate
concepts.explanation: A two-sided debate hands the thread from one speaker to the other: each side states a position, gives a reason, and responds; the concession (aunque) and the contrast (sin embargo, no obstante, en cambio) show who moved. Listen for the stance frames — creo que, en mi opinión, parece que — and the debate's last beat, the agreement, tells you who conceded what.

examples.target: Creo que la calle debería ser peatonal por las tardes.
examples.meaning: I think the street should be pedestrian in the afternoons.

examples.target: Sin embargo, mis clientes llegan en coche.
examples.meaning: However, my customers come by car.

examples.target: Aunque el reparto es un problema real, la calle puede abrirse.
examples.meaning: Although the deliveries are a real problem, the street can open.

examples.target: Parece que nos hemos puesto de acuerdo.
examples.meaning: It seems we have reached an agreement.

examples.target: En cambio, con horarios claros, ganamos todos.
examples.meaning: By contrast, with clear schedules, we all win.

concepts.commonError: Hearing the concession as a change of side: aunque gives the other side a point, it does not hand over the position — the contrast (sin embargo, en cambio) that follows shows where the speaker actually stands.

concepts.title: Leer dos posturas
concepts.explanation: A short article that presents two positions hands each idea to its speaker: según + the name says whose view it is. The organisation markers hold the structure — en primer lugar lists Vega's reasons, sin embargo and no obstante carry César's counter-reasons, and en cambio marks the difference between the two sides. The synthesis (al final, la conclusión) is where the article answers: who concedes what and what everyone gains.

examples.target: Según Vega, la calle peatonal vale la pena.
examples.meaning: According to Vega, the pedestrian street is worth it.

examples.target: Sin embargo, los clientes mayores llegan en coche.
examples.meaning: However, elderly customers come by car.

examples.target: En cambio, sin esos acuerdos, perdería clientes.
examples.meaning: By contrast, without those agreements, he would lose customers.

examples.target: Al final, los dos lados ceden un poco.
examples.meaning: In the end, both sides give ground a little.

examples.target: La conclusión es que todos ganan algo.
examples.meaning: The conclusion is that everyone gains something.

concepts.commonError: Mixing the two positions when the article hands them back: según Vega and según César say exactly who thinks what — read the source markers before you decide what the writer believes.

concepts.title: Mediar un desacuerdo
