hints: The bill request from «Prices and paying»: two words plus por favor — La cuenta, por favor.
activities.feedback: La cuenta, por favor. — mission complete: you found the café, ordered politely, and paid.

errors.explanation: The polite line keeps por favor: La cuenta, por favor.
La belongs with cuenta — the bill is la cuenta: La cuenta, por favor.
Por favor is two separate words.

activities.body: No new words today — this lesson is pure memory. Every answer comes from a lesson you have already finished: «First words», «Introducing yourself», «Days and times», and «Family and people». Each prompt names the lesson where you first met the answer. If you hesitate, think back to that lesson before you guess.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «First words». How do you say 'thank you'?
hints: The thanks word from «First words» is Gracias. Por favor is the asking-politely word.
activities.feedback: Gracias — one of your very first Spanish words, and still the most useful.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Introducing yourself». Complete the sentence.
hints: The introduction frame starts with the me that means 'myself': Me llamo.
activities.feedback: Me llamo — literally 'I call myself', the way Spanish introduces a name.

errors.explanation: Mi is 'my'; the introduction needs the reflexive Me: Me llamo Ana.
Yo would be an explicit subject; the name frame uses Me llamo — the me is part of the verb phrase.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Introducing yourself». Someone asks «¿Cómo te llamas?» — answer that your name is Ana.
hints: The full frame: Me llamo + the name. Me and the verb are a fixed pair.
activities.feedback: Me llamo Ana. — the full introduction, rebuilt from memory.

errors.explanation: Llamo is the I-form that pairs with me; llama is the he/she form.
Soy Ana is a valid introduction, but the question asks for the ¿Cómo te llamas? reply — Me llamo Ana.
That is a valid but bookish alternative; the lesson's frame for the question is Me llamo Ana.
Yo is optional and not part of the frame — Me llamo Ana stands alone.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Days and times». Which word means 'tomorrow'?
hints: Tomorrow is mañana — the one with the ñ. Hoy is today; el lunes is Monday.
activities.feedback: Mañana — and mind the ñ, it is not a plain n.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Family and people». Complete the phrase — it means 'the parents'.
hints: Padres is plural and masculine — the article is los. La would be singular feminine.
activities.feedback: Los padres — los for the plural, the way «Family and people» taught it.

errors.explanation: Padres is plural — more than one parent — so the article is los.
Padres is plural, so the article must be plural too: los padres.
Unos would mean 'some parents'; the phrase means THE parents — los padres.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Introducing yourself». Put the words in order to ask someone's name.
hints: The question opens with ¿Cómo, te comes next, and llamas closes it: ¿Cómo te llamas?
activities.feedback: ¿Cómo te llamas? — exactly as the lesson taught it.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Introducing yourself». Which of these means 'nice to meet you'?
hints: The meeting-pleasure phrase is Mucho gusto. The other options are introductions or questions.
activities.feedback: Mucho gusto — literally 'much pleasure', the standard reply after an introduction.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «First words». Say 'yes, thank you'.
hints: Two words from «First words» in order: Sí for yes, then gracias for thanks.
activities.feedback: Sí, gracias. — two of your very first Spanish words, still together.

errors.explanation: The pair runs emphatic-first: Sí, gracias — the yes comes before the thanks.
Yes needs its accent: Sí. Si without it means 'if'.

activities.prompt: Last one, from «Family and people». Which means 'the sister'?
hints: Sister is feminine — la hermana. El hermano is the brother; los padres are the parents.
activities.feedback: La hermana — la for feminine, hermana for sister. Four lessons revisited, nothing new added.

activities.body: You are in Madrid and the museum closes at six. Your phone is dead, so your Spanish has to do the work. Your mission has four parts: ask a passerby where the museum is, follow the directions you are given, ask the price of a ticket, and thank the cashier. Everything you need was taught in «Asking the way» and «Prices and paying». Read the mission card, then go.

activities.prompt: You stop a passerby. Which question asks where the museum is?
hints: Dónde opens a where-question and el museo names the target. ¿Cuánto cuesta? asks the price — you will need it at the ticket desk, not on the street.
activities.feedback: ¿Dónde? opens a where-question and el museo names your target. ¿Cuánto cuesta? asks the price — useful later, not now.

activities.prompt: Complete the question. Notice the accent — it is the same word you learned in «Asking the way».
hints: The blank holds the asking word that means 'where' — the same accent-carrying word from «Asking the way» and the earlier mission steps.
activities.feedback: Dónde with the accent means 'where'. Without it, donde is a different, plain word — the accent carries the meaning.

errors.explanation: Qué is 'what' — the place question needs the where-word: ¿Dónde está el museo?
Cómo is 'how'. Asking where the museum is takes dónde: ¿Dónde está el museo?

activities.prompt: The passerby says: «A la derecha, luego todo recto.» What do you do first?
hints: Derecha is 'right', and it comes before luego ('then') — you turn right first, then go straight ahead.
activities.feedback: A la derecha comes first — you turn right, and only luego, afterwards, do you go todo recto. Order matters in directions.

options.text: Go back the way you came

activities.prompt: You took a wrong turn. A shopkeeper points and says the museum is on the left. Complete the direction you hear.
hints: The shopkeeper points left — 'to the left' is a la izquierda, the twin of the derecha you just followed.
activities.feedback: A la izquierda — left. Keep it next to its twin a la derecha and you can follow almost any direction in Spain.

errors.explanation: Derecha is 'right' — the museum is on the left, so the word is izquierda.
Direction phrases use the fixed feminine form a la izquierda; izquierdo pairs with masculine nouns (el lado izquierdo).

activities.prompt: You reach the ticket desk. Which question asks the price of a ticket?
hints: Price questions use ¿Cuánto cuesta? — 'how much does it cost?' — the phrase from «Prices and paying». La cuenta belongs to a café table, not a ticket desk.
activities.feedback: ¿Cuánto cuesta? asks 'how much does it cost?' — you learned it in «Prices and paying». La cuenta is the bill at a café, not a ticket desk.

activities.prompt: The cashier answers «Son diez euros.» and hands you the ticket. What do you say?
hints: The ticket is in your hand — that is the moment for gracias. Hola was for arriving; mucho gusto is for meeting someone new.
activities.feedback: Gracias thanks — exactly the moment it was made for. Hola greets on arrival; mucho gusto is for meeting people, not tickets.

activities.prompt: Say the question to yourself, then type it: ask where the museum is.
hints: The question from step 2, straight from memory: ¿Dónde está el museo? — same words, same order, same accent.
activities.feedback: ¿Dónde está el museo? — the same question that started your mission. Notice how much faster it comes now.

errors.explanation: The article el sits between the verb and the museum: ¿Dónde está el museo?
Position takes estar, not ser: ¿Dónde está el museo?
Museo is masculine — its article is el, not la: ¿Dónde está el museo?

activities.prompt: Mission complete — you are inside the museum. You spot a friend across the hall: greet them, and thank the passerby who helped you. Type both.
hints: Two one-word lines: Hola. for your friend across the hall, Gracias. for the passerby who pointed you here.
activities.feedback: Hola greets, Gracias thanks — the two smallest words in your Spanish, and the two you will use most.

errors.explanation: Both parts of the mission close matter — the thank-you is missing: Hola. Gracias.
The greeting is missing: greet your friend first, then thank — Hola. Gracias.
Adiós is goodbye — you are greeting your friend, so open with Hola: Hola. Gracias.

activities.body: Your friend has invited you to a birthday party, and your brother and sister are coming too. Your mission has five parts: greet the host, introduce yourself, ask two guests their names, introduce your brother and your sister, and answer mucho gusto like you mean it. Everything you need was taught in «Introducing yourself» and «Family and people». Read the mission card, then walk in.

activities.prompt: You arrive at the door. Which word greets the host?
hints: You have just arrived — the universal opener is hola; adiós is what you say when you leave.
activities.feedback: Hola opens every Spanish conversation — say it the moment you arrive, not when you leave. That is what adiós is for.

activities.prompt: The host asks your name. Build the answer: 'My name is Leo.'
hints: The answer opens with the pronoun Me, then the verb llamo, then your name: Me llamo Leo.
activities.feedback: Me llamo Leo — literally 'I call myself Leo'. The me points back at you; that little pronoun is doing the real work.

activities.prompt: Now you want to know the guest's name. Which question do you ask?
hints: Flip the pronoun: me is for yourself (Me llamo), te points at the other person — ¿Cómo te llamas?
activities.feedback: ¿Cómo te llamas? — me llamo says my name, te llamas asks yours. Never swap me and te.

activities.prompt: The guest answers, and you reply politely. Complete the phrase.
hints: The fixed closer that means 'much pleasure' — the missing noun is gusto.
activities.feedback: Mucho gusto — 'much pleasure'. It is the handshake of Spanish small talk; use it with every new name.

errors.explanation: Mucho gracias is not a phrase — the reply to a new name is mucho gusto ('much pleasure').
The fixed phrase uses the noun gusto ('pleasure'); gusta is a verb form — the closer is Mucho gusto.

activities.prompt: Your sister Ana arrives. Introduce her — build: 'The sister is Ana.'
hints: Start with the feminine article La, then hermana, then es, then her name: La hermana es Ana.
activities.feedback: La hermana es Ana — la because hermana is feminine. The article and the noun always travel together and always agree.

activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly says the brother is Leo?
hints: Hermano is masculine, so its article must agree: El hermano es Leo. La would need a sister, los a plural.
activities.feedback: El hermano — masculine article with a masculine noun. La hermana would need a sister, and los needs a plural.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence about your brother.
hints: The blank holds the masculine singular article that agrees with hermano — one brother, so not los.
activities.feedback: El hermano — el marks masculine singular. Say the pair together until el hermano feels like one word.

errors.explanation: La goes with feminine nouns (la hermana). Hermano is masculine — the article is El.
Los is plural ('the brothers'). One brother takes the singular article: El hermano.

activities.prompt: A new guest joins the party. Type the polite reply you give after hearing their name.
hints: The two-word closer from step 5, typed from memory: Mucho gusto.
activities.feedback: Mucho gusto. — two words, and you already own them.

errors.explanation: The phrase uses the noun gusto — gusta is a verb form. Say Mucho gusto.
Gracias thanks someone; the closer for a new name is mucho gusto.

activities.prompt: Mission complete — the party is in full swing. One last guest arrives and asks your name. Introduce yourself from memory.
hints: Either form you practiced works from memory: Me llamo Leo. or Soy Leo. — the pronoun version is the one this mission built.
activities.feedback: Me llamo Leo or Soy Leo — either opens the door. Notice which one your mouth reaches for first; that is the one you truly know.

errors.explanation: The reflexive verb needs its pronoun me — without it, the verb belongs to nobody: Me llamo Leo.
Llamo is the I-form; llama means he/she says. Talking about yourself, use Me llamo Leo.

activities.body: Spanish family sentences are small machines: a name or soy / me llamo up front, es to link the person, and an article that must match — el with hermano, la with hermana. You already know every part from «Introducing yourself» and «Family and people». This lesson just bolts them together. Notice the patterns in the examples, then build.

activities.prompt: Build the introduction: 'My name is Ana.'
hints: Me llamo is a fixed pair: Me first, then llamo, then the name last. The me never moves.
activities.feedback: Me llamo Ana — me, then llamo, then the name. That order never changes.

activities.prompt: Now build: 'I am the brother.'
hints: Soy opens, then the article-noun pair travels as a unit: el hermano.
activities.feedback: Soy el hermano — soy first, then the article-noun pair. El hermano travels as a unit.

activities.prompt: The noun is missing. Complete the sentence about the sister.
hints: The article La tells you the noun is feminine — hermana, not hermano. The article is a clue.
activities.feedback: La hermana — la told you the noun was feminine before you even read it. Articles are clues, not decoration.

errors.explanation: La demands a feminine noun: hermana. Hermano is masculine and takes el.
Es Ana is singular and the article La is singular — hermana with no final -s.

activities.prompt: Which article belongs with 'hermano'?
hints: Hermano is masculine and singular — that is el's job. Los is plural, la is feminine, and una is an indefinite article.
activities.feedback: El hermano — masculine singular takes el. Los is plural, la is feminine, and una is the wrong job entirely.

activities.prompt: Build the full sentence: 'The brother is Leo.'
hints: Subject first: El hermano as one unit, then es as the link, then the name Leo last.
activities.feedback: El hermano es Leo — subject first, es in the middle, the name last. Spanish links with es the way English links with 'is'.

activities.prompt: Type the introduction from memory: 'My name is Ana.'
hints: The order stays fixed when typing: Me, then llamo, then Ana — exactly three words, nothing extra.
activities.feedback: Me llamo Ana. — from tiles to typing; the sentence is yours now.

errors.explanation: Llamo is the I-form that pairs with me; llama is the he/she form. It is always me llamo.
Yo is optional and the model frame omits it — Me llamo Ana is the complete introduction.
The pair stays in order: me llamo — me first, then llamo, then the name.

activities.prompt: The article is missing. Complete the sentence.
hints: Even after soy the article stays — hermano is masculine singular, so it keeps el.
activities.feedback: Soy el hermano — even after soy, the article stays. Spanish never drops it the way English drops 'the' in 'I am brother'.

errors.explanation: Hermano is masculine, so the article is el; la belongs with feminine nouns like hermana.
Hermano is singular — el. Los would make it plural: los hermanos.
Un would mean 'a brother'; the sentence needs the definite article — el hermano.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
hints: Article and noun must agree in gender and number: el with hermano, la with hermana — and es needs a singular subject.
activities.feedback: El hermano es Leo — every article agrees with its noun. In the wrong answers the article and the noun disagree, and Spanish ears catch it instantly.

activities.prompt: From memory: build 'Ana is the sister.'
hints: Same machine as before, from memory: Ana, then es, then the agreeing article-noun pair — la hermana.
activities.feedback: Ana es la hermana — name, es, article, noun. Four pieces, one pattern, and it works for your whole family.

activities.body: A Spanish noun never travels alone: it carries its article, and the article tells you the gender — el for masculine, la for feminine. In the plural they become los and las. And when the little words a and de meet el, they fuse: a + el is always al, de + el is always del.

activities.prompt: Cocina is feminine. Which article belongs with it?
hints: Cocina ends in -a and the moving-day tour introduced it as la cocina — the feminine singular article. El is masculine, and los/las are plural, so only la fits.
activities.feedback: Cocina is feminine and singular, so it takes la. El is masculine, and los and las are plural.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: the table is in the kitchen.
hints: Build it from left to right: mesa is feminine like cocina (la mesa), a location takes está (not es), and en means in — La mesa está en la cocina.
activities.feedback: Mesa is feminine, so la mesa; está places it, and en means in: La mesa está en la cocina.

answers: La mesa está en la cocina.

errors.answer: La mesa es en la cocina.
errors.explanation: Es says what a thing is; being in a place takes está: La mesa está en la cocina.
The room carries its article — en la cocina, not en cocina.

errors.answer: El mesa está en la cocina.
errors.explanation: Mesa is feminine, so la mesa — exactly like la cocina in the story.

activities.prompt: The contraction al is a + el fused. Choose the correct line for I'm going to the bathroom.
hints: The lesson's rule: a + el always fuses into al. Reject the option that splits them (a el), the one that reverses the trip (del = from the bathroom), and the gender mismatch (la baño) — only al survives.
activities.feedback: A + el always fuses into al — a el is never written. Del would mean from the bathroom, the opposite trip.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I come from the living room.
hints: Vengo is 'I come', and the little word de meets el and fuses — the story's evening walk used the same contraction: Vengo del salón.
activities.feedback: Vengo is I come, and de + el fuses: Vengo del salón.

errors.explanation: De + el never stay separate — they fuse into the single word del: Vengo del salón.
The fused de + el (del) belongs in the phrase: Vengo del salón.
Baño is the bathroom — the step asks for the living room, salón: Vengo del salón.

activities.prompt: Dormitorio is masculine. Fill the gap: ___ dormitorio es pequeño.
hints: The prompt already hands you the gender: dormitorio is masculine, and es pequeño is singular — that leaves the masculine singular article El.
activities.feedback: Dormitorio is masculine, so it takes el: El dormitorio es pequeño.

segments.text: Dormitorio is masculine. Fill the gap:

errors.explanation: Dormitorio is masculine, so it takes el, not la.
Es pequeño is singular, so the article is singular too: el, not los.
Las is the feminine plural; dormitorio is masculine and singular — El.

activities.body: Ser is the verb for describing: what something is like. El libro es nuevo, la casa es grande. The adjective is a mirror — it copies the noun's gender and number, so alto becomes alta and nuevo becomes nueva. Add muy in front and the description gets stronger: muy alto, very tall.

activities.prompt: Mesa is feminine. Which line describes it correctly?
hints: Mesa is feminine and singular, so the whole line mirrors it: la mesa es nueva. Nuevo on a feminine noun, or the masculine article el, breaks the mirror.
activities.feedback: Mesa is feminine and singular, so both the article and the adjective stay feminine: la mesa es nueva.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: the house is big.
hints: Ser carries the description and casa is feminine, but grande never changes for gender — it only grows a plural: La casa es grande.
activities.feedback: Casa is feminine, but grande is one of the adjectives that doesn't change for gender — only for number: La casa es grande.

errors.explanation: Casa is feminine, so the article is la: La casa es grande.
Son is the plural 'are'; one house is es: La casa es grande.
Muy means 'very' — the prompt just says big: La casa es grande.

activities.prompt: Muy always stands right before the adjective. Choose the correct line.
hints: Muy must stand directly before the adjective: Él es muy alto. Él muy es alto and es alto muy both put it in the wrong seat.
activities.feedback: Muy hugs the adjective it strengthens: es muy alto.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: the house is very big.
hints: Open with the article La, then casa, then es; muy hugs the adjective it strengthens and stands right before grande: La casa es muy grande.
activities.feedback: Ser carries the description, and muy stands before grande: La casa es muy grande.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: They are tall. (masculine)
hints: Ser's plural is son ('they are'), and the adjective joins the masculine plural: altos. And it is a description, so ser, not estar.
activities.feedback: Ser in the plural is son, and alto copies the masculine plural: Son altos.

errors.explanation: 'They' is plural, so the adjective must be plural too: Son altos.
The prompt says masculine — the adjective is altos, not the feminine alta.
Being tall is a description, not a temporary state — the verb is son, not están: Son altos.

activities.prompt: Libro is masculine and singular. Fill the gap: El libro es ___.
hints: Libro is masculine and singular, and the adjective copies it exactly: nuevo. Nueva, nuevos or nuevas would break the mirror.
activities.feedback: Libro is masculine and singular, so the adjective stays nuevo: El libro es nuevo.

segments.text: Libro is masculine and singular. Fill the gap: El libro es

errors.explanation: Libro is masculine, so the adjective stays nuevo, not nueva.
Es is singular — one book — so the adjective is singular too: nuevo.
Nuevas is feminine plural; libro is masculine singular: nuevo.

activities.prompt: Read the description. Which adjective describes the lamp?
hints: The last sentence of the description is about the lamp: La lámpara es alta. That sentence hands you the adjective.
activities.feedback: The last sentence gives it: la lámpara es alta.

errors.explanation: La cama es nueva — the bed is new. The lamp is the tall one: alta.
Grande describes the table, la mesa es grande. The lamp is alta.
Bonito describes the bedroom, mi dormitorio es pequeño pero bonito. The lamp is alta.

activities.body: Spanish plurals follow one friendly rule: a word ending in a vowel simply adds -s — libros, mesas. A word ending in a consonant adds -es — flores, ciudades — and lápiz politely changes its z to a c: lápices. Don't forget the article: el becomes los and la becomes las.

activities.prompt: Which is the correct plural of la flor?
hints: Flor ends in a consonant, so the plural takes -es — flores — and the feminine article stays las.
activities.feedback: Flor ends in a consonant, so it takes -es: las flores. Los would be masculine, which flor is not.

activities.prompt: Predict the phrase before you write it: two tables.
hints: Dos says two, mesa ends in a vowel, so the plural is mesas — no other ending needed.
activities.feedback: Mesa ends in a vowel, so the plural just adds -s: dos mesas.

errors.explanation: Dos demands the plural: dos mesas. The -s carries the 'two'.
The prompt asks for 'two tables' only — dos mesas. Grandes would say 'big tables'.
The prompt wants just 'two tables' — dos mesas; the article las is not asked for.

activities.prompt: Lápiz ends in z. Choose the correct plural line.
hints: Check all three agreements at once: the spelling change (lápices, not lápizs), the plural article los, and the plural adjective nuevos.
activities.feedback: The z becomes c before the -es ending, and the accent stays: los lápices.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: the flowers are pretty.
hints: Las flores is the plural subject (flor takes -es), son is the link, and the adjective agrees in number: bonitas.
activities.feedback: Flores is feminine plural, so the adjective follows: Las flores son bonitas.

activities.prompt: The colour tells you these are pencils. Fill the gap: Tres ___ rojos.
hints: Lápiz ends in z, so the z becomes c before the plural -es: lápices. The accent on the á stays.
activities.feedback: The z changes to c before -es: Tres lápices rojos.

segments.text: The colour tells you these are pencils. Fill the gap: Tres

errors.explanation: A -z noun does not take plain -s; the spelling changes first: lápiz → lápices.
The accent stays on the á even in the plural: lápices.
Tres means three — more than one pencil — so the plural lápices is needed.

activities.body: Regular -ar verbs are a small machine: remove -ar, then add -o for I and -a for he or she. Trabajo, trabaja; estudio, estudia. To say when, Spanish uses por with the part of day: por la mañana, por la tarde, por la noche — always por, never en.

activities.prompt: Which line correctly says I work in the morning?
hints: The I form of trabajar drops -ar and adds -o: trabajo. Mornings take the fixed phrase por la mañana — the other lines use the infinitive (trabajar), the wrong preposition (en), or drop the article (por mañana).
activities.feedback: The verb needs its -o ending, and the time phrase is fixed: Trabajo por la mañana.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: she studies in the afternoon.
hints: She takes the -a ending — estudia, like the sister in the story — and the afternoon phrase is por la tarde: Estudia por la tarde.
activities.feedback: Estudiar takes -a for she, and the afternoon is por la tarde: Estudia por la tarde.

errors.explanation: The infinitive estudiar needs its ending — she takes -a: Estudia por la tarde.
Spanish places parts of the day with por: por la tarde.
The time phrase keeps its article: por la tarde.

activities.prompt: The subject is yo. Choose the verb form that fits: ___ por la noche.
hints: Yo takes the -o ending — the story's alarm-clock machine works the same for trabajar and estudiar: trabajo, estudio. Trabaja is she, trabajan is they, trabajamos is we.
activities.feedback: For I, the -ar verb ends in -o: trabajo.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I study at night.
hints: Your I form of estudiar is estudio, and the night sits in the fixed por la noche phrase: Estudio por la noche.
activities.feedback: Estudio for I, and the night takes por: Estudio por la noche.

errors.explanation: The infinitive does not carry the -o ending you need: Estudio por la noche.
Parts of the day take por: Estudio por la noche.
The phrase keeps its article: por la noche.

activities.prompt: The subject is mi hermana, so the verb ends in -a. Fill the gap: Mi hermana ___ por la mañana.
hints: Mi hermana is 'she', and the prompt gives the ending: -a. The story's sister works with the same form — trabaja.
activities.feedback: For she, the -ar verb ends in -a: Mi hermana trabaja por la mañana.

segments.text: The subject is mi hermana, so the verb ends in -a. Fill the gap: Mi hermana

errors.explanation: Trabajo is the yo form ('I work'); mi hermana takes -a: trabaja.
The infinitive does not conjugate for a person — drop -ar and add -a: trabaja.
Trabajamos is 'we work'; one sister takes the singular -a form: trabaja.

activities.body: Saying no in Spanish is beautifully simple: put no right in front of the verb — no trabajo, no estudia. For extra shade, Spanish adds negative partners after the verb: nunca, nada, nadie. And where English forbids double negatives, Spanish welcomes them: No como nada is the natural way to say it.

activities.prompt: Which line correctly says I don't work?
hints: No needs a conjugated verb, not an infinitive, and it stands BEFORE the verb — No trabajo is the only line that does both.
activities.feedback: No stands before the conjugated verb: No trabajo.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: she doesn't study.
hints: No goes directly before the verb — No estudia. No ella needed; the verb carries the subject.
activities.feedback: No goes before estudia: No estudia.

errors.explanation: Estudiar is the infinitive; after no, the conjugated form is needed — No estudia.
Ella is optional — the verb already says she. The model frame is exactly No estudia.
Estudie is the formal/subjunctive form; the plain present she-form is estudia.

activities.prompt: Choose the correct negative line.
hints: Spanish doubles the negative happily: no before the verb, nada after it. Algo is the positive 'something' — the wrong partner for no.
activities.feedback: No and nada team up happily in Spanish: No como nada.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: I don't work at night.
hints: No leads the sentence and sticks right before the verb: No trabajo, then por la noche.
activities.feedback: No leads, right before the verb: No trabajo por la noche.

activities.prompt: Nobody is the subject, and it takes a singular verb. Fill the gap: ___ habla español en mi casa.
hints: The nobody word is nadie, and it keeps the singular verb habla. Nada is 'nothing' — it doesn't speak.
activities.feedback: Nadie is the nobody word, and it takes a singular verb: Nadie habla español.

segments.text: Nobody is the subject, and it takes a singular verb. Fill the gap:

errors.explanation: Nada means 'nothing' and wouldn't speak; the nobody who speaks is nadie.
Ninguno is 'none (of)' and needs a noun after it; the subject standing alone is nadie.

activities.prompt: Which question asks where someone lives?
hints: Dónde is the where-word. Qué, cómo and cuándo ask what, how and when — match the meaning, not the drill: where someone lives takes dónde.
activities.feedback: Dónde is the where word; qué asks what and cuándo asks when.

activities.prompt: Predict the question before you write it: what does he eat?
hints: Qué asks what, and comer for 'he' keeps the -e: come (comes is you). Write the full question — ¿Qué come? — with the accent on Qué.
activities.feedback: Qué asks what, and comer takes -e for he: ¿Qué come?

errors.explanation: Comer is the infinitive 'to eat'; the question asks what he eats, so it takes the conjugated form come: ¿Qué come?
Que without its accent means 'that'; the question word wears the accent — ¿Qué come?
Comen is 'they eat'; one person eats, so the verb stays come: ¿Qué come?
Como is 'I eat'; the question asks what HE eats — come: ¿Qué come?

activities.prompt: The accent carries the meaning. Choose the correct question.
hints: Cómo with its accent asks how. The reflexives already carry the person — me/te — so a stray tú before the verb is a giveaway: ¿Cómo te llamas?
activities.feedback: Cómo with the accent asks how; ¿Cómo tú te llamas? scrambles the order — pronouns don't need tú before them.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: Who works here?
hints: Quién asks who and never drops its accent. Trabajar for one person is trabaja (the -a ending), and here is aquí: ¿Quién trabaja aquí?
activities.feedback: Quién asks who, with its accent: ¿Quién trabaja aquí?

errors.explanation: Quien without the accent is the relative 'who/that'; the question word is quién, accent included.
Trabajar is the infinitive; who works needs the conjugated form: trabaja.
Allí means 'there'; the prompt asks about here — aquí: ¿Quién trabaja aquí?

activities.prompt: Read the note. Where is the party?
hints: The note answers its own question: ¿Dónde es? — Es en mi casa. The where is the place after en — mi casa.
activities.feedback: The answer follows the question directly: Es en mi casa.

errors.explanation: Ocho is when the party starts; the question asks WHERE it is — es en mi casa.
La familia answers who's coming; the where is en mi casa.
Su casa would be his or their house; the note says mi casa — my house.

activities.body: Comer and beber follow the regular -er pattern: como, comes, come and bebo, bebes, bebe. Then comes Spanish's famous backwards verb: me gusta. Think of it as the food pleasing you — Me gusta el pan — so the verb agrees with the food, not with you. Plural food, plural verb: Me gustan las frutas.

activities.prompt: Which line correctly says I like the bread?
hints: Liking runs backwards — the bread pleases me — so the verb stays gusta, matched to singular el pan. Me gusto turns it reflexive ('I please myself'), yo gusto drops the me, and pan without el loses its article.
activities.feedback: Gustar agrees with the bread — singular — so it stays gusta: Me gusta el pan.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: I drink water.
hints: Beber is a regular -er verb: your I form drops -er and adds -o — bebo. Water here is a general thing, so it travels bare: Bebo agua.
activities.feedback: Beber takes -o for I: Bebo agua.

errors.explanation: The infinitive beber needs its ending — your I form is bebo: Bebo agua.
Bebe is 'he/she drinks'; 'I drink' is bebo.
Water as a general thing takes no article here — the model is Bebo agua.

activities.prompt: The noun is plural, so the verb must be too. Choose the correct line.
hints: The dessert table made the fruit plural: las frutas, and the backwards verb agrees with it — gustan. Gusta is singular, me gusto is the reflexive slip, and me gustas addresses a person.
activities.feedback: Las frutas is plural, so gustar becomes gustan: Me gustan las frutas.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: She eats bread.
hints: Comer is a regular -er verb and she takes the -e ending: come. The bread is a general thing, so it travels bare — Come pan.
activities.feedback: Comer takes -e for she: Come pan.

errors.explanation: The infinitive does not conjugate — she takes -e: Come pan.
Como is 'I eat'; 'she eats' is come.
El pan is 'the bread'; general bread travels bare here: Come pan.

activities.prompt: The subject is yo, so the verb ends in -o. Fill the gap: Yo ___ agua por la mañana.
hints: The prompt gives the ending: yo takes -o, and the lesson's drinking verb is beber — its I form is bebo.
activities.feedback: The I form of beber is bebo: Yo bebo agua por la mañana.

segments.text: The subject is yo, so the verb ends in -o. Fill the gap: Yo

errors.explanation: Bebe is 'he/she drinks'; yo takes -o: bebo.
Drop -er for the conjugated form — yo bebo, not the infinitive.
Como is 'I eat' — the step asks for the drinking verb: bebo.

activities.body: Mi, tu and su are wonderfully low-maintenance: they never change for masculine or feminine — mi libro, mi casa. They only change for number, adding an -s for plurals: mis libros, tus casas, sus amigos. One warning: su does four jobs — his, her, your (formal) and their — so listen for context.

activities.prompt: Which line says your book using the informal tu?
hints: Libro is singular, so tu stays singular — no -s on the possessive — and it must be tu (your), not mi (my).
activities.feedback: Libro is singular, so tu stays singular too: Tu libro es nuevo.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: my friends live here.
hints: Amigos is plural: Mis amigos, then the plural verb viven, then aquí.
activities.feedback: Amigos is plural, so mi becomes mis: Mis amigos viven aquí.

errors.explanation: Amigos is plural, so the possessive joins it: Mis amigos.
Viven is the they-form; vive is for one person — Mis amigos viven.
The noun carries the plural too — Mis amigos, not Mis amigo.

activities.prompt: The noun is plural. Choose the possessive that matches: ___ casas son grandes.
hints: Casas is plural, so the possessive takes the -s: Mis. Mi, Mies and a singular noun are all wrong partners.
activities.feedback: Casas is plural, so the possessive takes -s: Mis casas son grandes.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: your table is in the kitchen.
hints: The possessive comes before the noun: Tu mesa, then está, then en la cocina. No article joins tu.
activities.feedback: Possessive first, then the noun: Tu mesa está en la cocina.

activities.prompt: Amigos is plural, so the possessive needs its -s. Fill the gap: ___ amigos son simpáticos.
hints: Amigos is plural, so the possessive needs its plural -s too: Mis amigos.
activities.feedback: Amigos is plural, so my becomes mis: Mis amigos son simpáticos.

segments.text: Amigos is plural, so the possessive needs its -s. Fill the gap:

errors.explanation: Amigos is plural, so the possessive must agree: Mis. Mi pairs with a singular noun.
Tus is 'your'; the sentence is about my friends — Mis amigos son simpáticos.
The possessive mis has no accent — Mís is not a word.

activities.body: Ir is the verb for going, and it's irregular in a friendly way: voy, vas, va, vamos, van. Getting there is just as easy: en plus the vehicle — en coche, en metro, en autobús. The one exception is your own two feet: a pie, on foot. And the destination follows a: Voy al centro.

activities.prompt: Which line says I go by subway?
hints: Your form of ir is voy, and vehicles ride on en — the story's first ride was en metro. Voy a metro uses the wrong preposition, Ir en metro is the bare infinitive, and the last option crams two trips into one line.
activities.feedback: Ir gives voy for I, and transport takes en: Voy en metro.

options.text: Voy en el metro a pie.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: we go on foot.
hints: The we form of ir is vamos, and on foot is the lesson's fixed phrase a pie — no vehicle, no en: Vamos a pie.
activities.feedback: The we form of ir is vamos, and on foot is the rebel a pie: Vamos a pie.

errors.explanation: Voy is 'I go'; for 'we go' ir gives vamos: Vamos a pie.
On foot is the fixed phrase a pie, not en pie.
A pie is a fixed expression with no article between: Vamos a pie.

activities.prompt: The subject is ella. Choose the form of ir that fits: Ella ___ al centro.
hints: Ir is irregular in a friendly way — voy, vas, va — and for ella the form is va, the very one the story's sister used driving through the traffic.
activities.feedback: For he/she, ir is va: Ella va al centro.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: He goes to Madrid by car.
hints: Ir gives va for he, the destination takes a (va a Madrid), and the car rides on en (en coche) — in that order: Va a Madrid en coche.
activities.feedback: Va for he, a for the destination, en for the car: Va a Madrid en coche.

answers: Él va a Madrid en coche.

errors.explanation: Voy is 'I go'; 'he goes' is va: Va a Madrid en coche.
The destination needs the little word a: Va a Madrid.
Vehicles ride on en, not a: Va a Madrid en coche.

activities.prompt: You want to ask how. Fill the gap: ¿___ vas al trabajo?
hints: All morning the story asked ¿cómo voy? — 'how' is cómo (with its accent), and here it pairs with vas: ¿Cómo vas al trabajo?
activities.feedback: Cómo asks how: ¿Cómo vas al trabajo?

segments.text: You want to ask how. Fill the gap: ¿

errors.explanation: Cuánto asks 'how much'; the question word for 'how' is cómo: ¿Cómo vas al trabajo?
Without its accent, como means 'as' or 'I eat' — the question word carries it: Cómo.

activities.prompt: Which is the most polite way to ask for the bill?
hints: Rank the softness: querría + por favor is the polite peak. Quiero ya and dame are brusque commands, and La cuenta quiero puts the verb last — the odd one out.
activities.feedback: Querría softens the request into would-like: Querría la cuenta, por favor.

activities.prompt: Predict the question before you write it: can you help me? (informal)
hints: Poder for you (informal) is puedes — the -es ending. Help me is one glued word, ayudarme, with me riding the infinitive: ¿Puedes ayudarme?
activities.feedback: Poder takes -es for you, and ayudarme is help-me in one word: ¿Puedes ayudarme?

errors.explanation: Puede is the polite he/she/usted form; the prompt says informal you — puedes.
Puedo is 'I can' and te is 'you'; the question is reversed — can YOU help ME: ¿Puedes ayudarme?
Ayúdame is the command form; after puedes the helper stays the bare infinitive: ayudarme.
Le is 'him/her'; the prompt asks can you help ME — me: ¿Puedes ayudarme?

activities.prompt: After poder comes the infinitive. Choose the correct line.
hints: Poder hands off to the bare infinitive: puedo ir. Voy (a conjugation), ido (a participle) and yendo (a gerund) are all wrong after puedo.
activities.feedback: Poder is always followed by the plain infinitive: Puedo ir mañana.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I would like a coffee, please.
hints: Would-like is the conditional querría — querer softened. Un café, and por favor to close it politely: Querría un café, por favor.
activities.feedback: Querría is the polite conditional of querer: Querría un café, por favor.

errors.explanation: Quiero is a plain want; the prompt's 'would like' is the softened conditional — querría.
The courtesy marker belongs to the line: por favor — Querría un café, por favor.
Café is masculine: un café, never una café.
Quería is the past 'I wanted'; the would-like form is querría — the conditional with its double r.

activities.prompt: Read the café exchange. What does Ana order?
hints: Ana's first line is her order: Querría un café, por favor. The café is what she asks for; the card question and the waiter's offers are the rest.
activities.feedback: Her first line places the order: Querría un café, por favor.

errors.explanation: La cuenta comes up in the card question later; what Ana ORDERS is the café.
The exchange never mentions tea — Ana's order is un café, por favor.
Ana declines only the waiter's extra offer; her order itself is un café.

activities.body: The past tense in Spanish is refreshingly regular to start: -ar verbs take -é for I — hablé, trabajé, estudié — and -er/-ir verbs take -í — comí, viví. Then memorise one small giant: fue, which means both was and went. Set the scene with ayer or anoche, and you're telling stories.

activities.prompt: Which line says I spoke with Ana yesterday?
hints: The I-form of the past ends in -é with its accent: hablé. Hablo is present 'I speak', hablar the infinitive and hablado the participle — only hablé fits yesterday.
activities.feedback: The -é ending with its accent is the I form of the past: Ayer hablé con Ana.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: I ate bread.
hints: Comer is an -er verb, so 'I' in the past ends in -í: comí. The accent lands on the final vowel.
activities.feedback: Comer is an -er verb, so the I past ends in -í: Comí pan.

errors.explanation: Como is the present 'I eat'; the story is in the past — Comí pan.
Comer is the untouched infinitive; the sentence needs the past I-form: Comí pan.
The dictated sentence is bare — no article before pan: Comí pan.

activities.prompt: Fue means was here. Choose the correct line.
hints: Fue already means 'was' — it never needs a helper verb. Es fue, era fue and fui all pile up verbs; the single word fue carries the whole meaning.
activities.feedback: Fue already means was — no helper verb needed: La película fue muy buena.

options.text: La película es fue muy buena.
La película era fue muy buena.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: last night I studied Spanish.
hints: Time expression first — Anoche — then the past verb estudié, then what was studied: español. Anoche estudié español.
activities.feedback: Time first, then the past verb: Anoche estudié español.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: Yesterday I worked a lot.
hints: Ayer sets the scene first, then the past verb trabajé with its accent, then mucho: time first, verb second.
activities.feedback: Ayer sets the past, and trabajé carries the accent: Ayer trabajé mucho.

errors.explanation: Trabajo is the present; the sentence is about yesterday — Ayer trabajé mucho.
Trabajó is 'he/she worked'; the prompt says 'I' — Ayer trabajé mucho.
The lesson's rule puts time first: Ayer trabajé mucho.

activities.prompt: The subject is yo, so the past of hablar ends in -é. Fill the gap: Ayer ___ con mi madre.
hints: The prompt says the subject is yo: hablar's yo past is hablé — the -é with its accent. Hablo would be the present.
activities.feedback: The I past of hablar is hablé: Ayer hablé con mi madre.

segments.text: The subject is yo, so the past of hablar ends in -é. Fill the gap: Ayer

errors.explanation: Hablo is the present 'I speak'; yesterday calls the past form hablé.
Hablaba is the stretched habit-tense; a done-and-dusted single action takes hablé.
The yo past carries its accent: hablé.

activities.prompt: Read about yesterday. Who did the writer speak with?
hints: The passage says it in the afternoon line: Por la tarde hablé con Ana. The writer spoke with Ana — not with the family they ate with.
activities.feedback: The third sentence names her: hablé con Ana.

errors.explanation: The writer ATE with the family — Comí con mi familia. The speaking partner was Ana.
No one speaks with a mother here — the passage names Ana: hablé con Ana.
The writer studied a little at night, but the question asks who they spoke with: Ana.

activities.body: Spanish weather is made, not been: Hace sol, Hace calor, Hace frío — literally it makes sun, heat, cold. When the sky is cloudy, Spanish switches to estar: Está nublado. And the four seasons — primavera, verano, otoño, invierno — are masculine except la primavera.

activities.prompt: Which line says it's sunny?
hints: Sunny is made, not been — the story's beach-plan opener used hace sol. Es and está try to 'be' the weather, and hace soleado forces the adjective Spanish doesn't use here.
activities.feedback: Sunny weather is made with hacer: Hace sol.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: it's cold.
hints: Cold is made too: the formula is hace + the weather noun, like the story's mountain line — Hace frío, with the accent on frío.
activities.feedback: Cold is made, not been: Hace frío.

errors.explanation: Cold is made with hacer, not estar: Hace frío.
Caliente is the adjective 'hot'; the cold here is the noun frío: Hace frío.
Frío carries its accent: Hace frío.

activities.prompt: Choose the correct line about summer.
hints: Summer sits in en verano, the heat is made with hace (never es or hay here), and the noun is calor — not the adjective caliente: En verano hace mucho calor.
activities.feedback: Hacer carries the weather noun calor: En verano hace mucho calor.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: It's cloudy.
hints: Cloudy is the one weather that switches to estar — está, with its accent — plus the nublado from the story's Valencia forecast: Está nublado.
activities.feedback: Cloudy skies take estar: Está nublado.

errors.explanation: Cloudy skies take estar, not hacer: Está nublado.
Cloudiness is a state, so estar: Está nublado.
Está carries its accent on the a: Está nublado.

activities.prompt: Cloudy skies take estar, not hacer. Fill the gap: Hoy ___ nublado.
hints: The prompt gives the rule and the partner: cloudy skies take estar, and the story's Valencia forecast used the same form — está, accent on the a.
activities.feedback: Cloudy skies take estar: Hoy está nublado.

segments.text: Cloudy skies take estar, not hacer. Fill the gap: Hoy

errors.explanation: Cloudiness is a state, so estar, not ser: está nublado.
Cloudy skies are the exception that takes estar, not hacer: está nublado.
The form of estar needs its accent: está.

activities.body: Spanish months are humble: masculine, and always lowercase — enero, mayo, diciembre. Dates flip the English order: the day comes first with el, then de, then the month — el 3 de mayo. Your birthday fits the same frame: Mi cumpleaños es el 5 de enero.

activities.prompt: Which line writes the date correctly?
hints: A Spanish date needs its el before the day and de before the month: el 3 de mayo. Missing either piece, or flipping the order, breaks the frame.
activities.feedback: The day needs its el and the month its de: el 3 de mayo.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: my birthday is in June.
hints: For the month alone, en is enough: en junio. The birthday equals a date, so it rides ser: Mi cumpleaños es en junio.
activities.feedback: For the month alone, en is enough: Mi cumpleaños es en junio.

errors.explanation: The month needs its preposition en: es en junio.
Birthdays and dates ride ser — es, not está.
The prompt asks for June; enero is a different month — Mi cumpleaños es en junio.

activities.prompt: Months stay lowercase. Choose the correct line.
hints: Months never take a capital in Spanish: diciembre. The correct line writes it lower-case and needs no el after en.
activities.feedback: Diciembre never takes a capital: La fiesta es en diciembre.

options.text: La fiesta es en el diciembre.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: my birthday is January 5th.
hints: Possessor first — Mi cumpleaños — then es, then the date frame el + cinco + de + enero. Day before month: el cinco de enero.
activities.feedback: El 5 de enero — day first: Mi cumpleaños es el cinco de enero.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: Today is May 3rd.
hints: Hoy es, then the date with its el and de: el tres de mayo. The day comes first, the month after de — never the English order.
activities.feedback: Day with el, month with de: Hoy es el tres de mayo.

answers: Hoy es el tres de mayo.

errors.explanation: The month needs its de: el 3 de mayo.
Spanish dates put the day first with el, then de, then the month: el 3 de mayo.
The date frame carries its el: Hoy es el tres de mayo.

activities.prompt: The month is June, always lowercase. Fill the gap: El concierto es el 20 de ___.
hints: The month stays lower-case — junio — and takes no article after de. The frame is el 20 de junio.
activities.feedback: Lowercase, as always: El concierto es el 20 de junio.

segments.text: The month is June, always lowercase. Fill the gap: El concierto es el 20 de

errors.explanation: The concert is June 20th — the month is junio, not enero.
After de, the month walks alone — no article: el 20 de junio.
Junio is June, the month in the prompt. Julio is July — a different date.

activities.prompt: Read the birthday note. When is the writer's birthday?
hints: The note opens with the birthday: Mi cumpleaños es el 5 de enero. The party on the 10th and the family months are decoys.
activities.feedback: The first sentence gives the date: el 5 de enero.

errors.explanation: The 10th is the party, not the birthday. The birthday is el 5 de enero.
June is the sister's birthday month. The writer's own birthday is el 5 de enero.
December belongs to the parents. The writer's birthday is el 5 de enero.

activities.prompt: Which line correctly asks for half a kilo of cheese?
hints: The quantity medio kilo is joined to the food with de, and nothing else gets added — no un, no el: Medio kilo de queso, por favor.
activities.feedback: Medio kilo is already the quantity, and it needs de: Medio kilo de queso, por favor.

options.text: Medio kilo de queso, por favor.
Un medio kilo de queso, por favor.
Medio kilo del queso, por favor.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: a bottle of water, please.
hints: You met this buy in the earlier steps: feminine Una + botella + de + agua, closed with por favor.
activities.feedback: Botella is feminine — una — and the water follows de: Una botella de agua, por favor.

answers: Una botella de agua, por favor.

errors.answer: Un botella de agua, por favor.
errors.explanation: Botella is feminine — it takes una, not un: Una botella de agua, por favor.
The courteous closer por favor belongs on the request: Una botella de agua, por favor.
The de links the container to its content: botella de agua.

activities.prompt: Pan is masculine. Choose the correct pointer.
hints: Masculine nouns point with este. Pan is masculine, so the pointer is Este — not Esta (feminine), not Esto (neuter).
activities.feedback: Masculine nouns point with este: Este pan está fresco.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: I want a kilo of apples.
hints: Lead with Quiero, then the quantity un kilo, then the linker de, then the fruit manzanas.
activities.feedback: Quiero, then the quantity with its de: Quiero un kilo de manzanas.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: This bread is fresh.
hints: Este for masculine pan; being fresh right now is a state, so the verb is estar: Este pan está fresco.
activities.feedback: Este for the masculine pan, and fresh is a state — estar: Este pan está fresco.

errors.explanation: Pan is masculine, so the pointer is este, not esta: Este pan está fresco.
Es says what something is; for how the bread is right now (fresh), Spanish uses estar: Este pan está fresco.
Esto is the neuter form and stands alone; pointing at a noun (pan) takes the masculine Este pan.

activities.prompt: You want a bottle. Fill the gap: Una ___ de agua, por favor.
hints: The gap is the market container for water — 'a ___ of water': the feminine noun botella.
activities.feedback: The bottle word is botella: Una botella de agua, por favor.

segments.text: You want a bottle. Fill the gap: Una

errors.explanation: The Spanish word for bottle is botella: Una botella de agua, por favor.
Bolsa is a bag — the market container for water is una botella.

activities.body: Spanish pain is backwards, just like Spanish liking: Me duele la cabeza — literally, the head hurts to me. One aching part takes duele; several take duelen: Me duelen las manos. And body parts wear the article, not a possessive: la cabeza, las manos. When it's serious: Voy al médico.

activities.prompt: Which line says my head hurts?
hints: Pain runs backwards like liking: me + duele — the head hurts to me. The other lines use the wrong reflexive (me duelo), a possessive (mi cabeza), or scramble the order (Duele me).
activities.feedback: Doler works like gustar — duele agrees with la cabeza — and body parts take the article: Me duele la cabeza.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: my hands hurt.
hints: Las manos is plural, so the backwards verb stretches into duelen — the story's noon line used the same switch: Me duelen las manos.
activities.feedback: Las manos is plural, so doler becomes duelen: Me duelen las manos.

errors.explanation: Las manos is plural, so the verb agrees and becomes duelen: Me duelen las manos.
Manos is feminine, so its plural article is las: las manos.
Me duelo would be 'I hurt myself' — the hands hurt, so duele's plural: duelen.

activities.prompt: The noun is singular. Choose the verb that matches: Me ___ el estómago.
hints: El estómago is singular, so the backwards verb stays duele — the form the clinic scene used; duelen would need several body parts, and me duelo is the reflexive slip.
activities.feedback: El estómago is singular, so duele stays singular: Me duele el estómago.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I have a fever.
hints: Spanish carries a fever with tener, it doesn't be it — your form is tengo, and the fever rides bare: Tengo fiebre.
activities.feedback: Spanish has a fever rather than being feverish: Tengo fiebre.

errors.explanation: A fever is carried with tener, not estar: Tengo fiebre.
Fiebre here is a general condition and takes no article: Tengo fiebre.
The infinitive needs its ending — your I form is tengo: Tengo fiebre.

activities.prompt: Body parts take the article, not a possessive. Fill the gap: Me duele ___.
hints: The prompt states the rule: the article, not a possessive. The part that woke Pablo up wrong was la cabeza — Me duele la cabeza.
activities.feedback: The article, not a possessive, with body parts: Me duele la cabeza.

segments.text: Body parts take the article, not a possessive. Fill the gap: Me duele

errors.explanation: Spanish uses the article, not a possessive, with body parts: la cabeza.
Cabeza is feminine — the article is la: la cabeza.
The body part keeps its article: la cabeza.

activities.prompt: Which line correctly asks for something for a headache?
hints: Ask with Tiene (the formal you), then algo, then para for 'for', then el dolor de cabeza. The traps swap para for por or drop the article.
activities.feedback: Para marks purpose, and de cabeza completes the phrase: ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de cabeza?

options.text: ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de cabeza?
¿Tiene algo por el dolor de cabeza?
¿Necesito algo para el dolor de cabeza?

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: I need these pills.
hints: State the need in one line: Necesito + the feminine plural pointer estas + pastillas.
activities.feedback: Necesito plus the noun: Necesito estas pastillas.

errors.explanation: Pastillas is plural, so the pointer must agree: estas pastillas.
Pastillas is feminine — the plural pointer is estas, not estos.
The pointer estas ('these') points at the pills you need: Necesito estas pastillas.

activities.prompt: Purpose takes para. Choose the correct line.
hints: Only the purpose word decides this one: para marks 'for the purpose of' — not por, not de, not a.
activities.feedback: Para means for the purpose of: Algo para la fiebre, por favor.

options.text: Algo para la fiebre, por favor.
Algo por la fiebre, por favor.
Algo de la fiebre, por favor.
Algo a la fiebre, por favor.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: do you have something for the pain? (formal)
hints: Open with ¿Tiene, then algo, then the purpose linker para, then el dolor.
activities.feedback: ¿Tiene algo para el dolor? — tiene for the formal you, para for purpose.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I need a prescription.
hints: Necesito + una + receta — receta is feminine, so the article is una.
activities.feedback: Necesito plus the noun: Necesito una receta.

errors.explanation: Receta is feminine — it takes una, not un: Necesito una receta.
The article una belongs in front of receta: Necesito una receta.

activities.prompt: The pharmacy is close by. Fill the gap: La farmacia está ___.
hints: 'The pharmacy is ___' — the gap word means 'nearby'; you are almost there.
activities.feedback: Cerca means nearby: La farmacia está cerca.

segments.text: The pharmacy is close by. Fill the gap: La farmacia está

errors.explanation: Lejos means 'far' — the pharmacy is close by, which is cerca.
Cercano is an adjective that describes a noun; after está you need the adverb cerca ('nearby').

activities.body: Emergencies run on short, strong phrases: ¡Socorro! and Necesito ayuda. The command to call for help uses the formal form — ¡Llame a una ambulancia! — because emergencies are no place for casual speech. And the number to know across all of Europe is 112.

activities.prompt: Which line gives the formal command to call an ambulance?
hints: Emergencies use the formal command: Llame with -e. Llama is the tú form, Llame una drops the needed a, and Llamar is the bare infinitive.
activities.feedback: Llame is the formal command, and llamar needs its a: Llame a una ambulancia.

activities.prompt: Predict the question before you write it: where is the hospital?
hints: Dónde takes its accent, está says where something is, and the hospital needs its article: ¿Dónde está el hospital?
activities.feedback: Dónde with its accent, está for location: ¿Dónde está el hospital?

errors.explanation: Location takes estar, not ser: ¿Dónde está el hospital?
The hospital needs its article el: ¿Dónde está el hospital?
Dónde carries its accent when it asks where: ¿Dónde está el hospital?

activities.prompt: Emergencies use the formal command. Choose the correct cry.
hints: The formal command is Llame — the usted form. Llamo means 'I call' (useless when asking for help), and Llamar/Llames are the wrong shape for a command.
activities.feedback: Llame is the usted command — Llamo would mean I call, which helps nobody.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: call an ambulance, please.
hints: The formal command Llame leads, then a + una + ambulancia, then por favor to soften it: Llame a una ambulancia, por favor.
activities.feedback: The command first, then a una ambulancia: Llame a una ambulancia, por favor.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I need help!
hints: Necesito + ayuda — no article in between — and the exclamation marks frame the cry: ¡Necesito ayuda!
activities.feedback: Necesito ayuda, with the marks that frame it: ¡Necesito ayuda!

errors.explanation: Ayudas is 'you help'; the noun is ayuda: ¡Necesito ayuda!
The cry carries no article: Necesito ayuda. La ayuda would mean a specific help.
Ayuda is feminine and takes no article in this cry: Necesito ayuda.

activities.prompt: This is the cry for help. Fill the gap: ¡___!
hints: This is the standalone shout for help — the intro's very first phrase: ¡Socorro!
activities.feedback: ¡Socorro! is the cry for help.

segments.text: This is the cry for help. Fill the gap: ¡

errors.explanation: ¡Ayuda! is the other cry of the lesson, but the taught shout for help is ¡Socorro!.
Llame starts the command 'Llame a una ambulancia'; the bare cry for help is ¡Socorro!.
Emergencia names the situation, not the cry. The shout is ¡Socorro!.

activities.prompt: Read the emergency. What does the woman call?
hints: The passage names her action: Una mujer llama a una ambulancia. The man shouts ¡Socorro! — the woman calls the ambulance.
activities.feedback: The second sentence says it: llama a una ambulancia.

errors.explanation: No police here — the woman calls a una ambulancia.
Socorro is the man's shout; the woman calls an ambulance.
112 is the number to know, but the passage says the woman calls a una ambulancia.

activities.prompt: Which line accepts the invitation?
hints: Accepting is a warm yes: ¡Claro que sí! Claro que no refuses, and Lo siento declines — the yes-line is the one with gracias.
activities.feedback: ¡Claro que sí! is the warm yes; Lo siento, no puedo is the gentle no.

activities.prompt: Predict the question before you write it: do you want to come? (informal)
hints: Querer for you (informal) is quieres — the -es ending. After it comes the bare infinitive: venir → ¿Quieres venir?
activities.feedback: Querer takes -es for you: ¿Quieres venir?

errors.explanation: Quiere is the polite he/she/usted form; the prompt says informal you — quieres: ¿Quieres venir?
After quieres the second verb stays the bare infinitive: venir, not a second conjugation.
Ir is 'to go'; the invitation says come — venir: ¿Quieres venir?

activities.prompt: Invitar needs its a. Choose the correct invitation.
hints: Invitar always takes the preposition a: te invito a + place. En says 'inside', de says 'from' — the invitation preposition is a.
activities.feedback: The a bridges invito to the place: Te invito a mi casa.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I'm sorry, I can't.
hints: The gentle decline is two beats: Lo siento (I'm sorry) + no puedo (I can't). Poder for I is puedo — o turns ue — and no rides before the verb.
activities.feedback: The gentle decline: Lo siento, no puedo.

errors.explanation: No poder is the infinitive; the line needs the conjugated I form — no puedo.
No rides before the verb: no puedo. 'Puedo no' scrambles the negation.
The apology is two words in Spanish — lo siento; the lo belongs: Lo siento, no puedo.
Puedas is the subjunctive; a plain statement of can't takes puedo.

activities.prompt: Read the invitation. Does Pablo accept?
hints: Pablo's line answers the question outright: ¡Claro que sí, gracias! — the warm yes. The passage's dialogue settles it in its second line.
activities.feedback: His answer is the warm yes: ¡Claro que sí, gracias!

errors.explanation: Pablo answers ¡Claro que sí, gracias! — he is coming.
Lo siento is the decline; Pablo accepts with the warm ¡Claro que sí!
Claro que no is the refusal; Pablo's answer is Claro que sí.

activities.body: The past in Spanish is a habit, not a rule to memorize. For things that are done and dusted, -ar verbs take -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -aron (hablé, hablaste, habló) and -er/-ir verbs take -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -ieron (comí, comiste, comió). Then there are the rebels you will use every day — tuve, hice, dije, estuvo — no pattern, just friends you memorize by meeting them.

activities.prompt: Which ending marks the yo form of -ar verbs in the past?
hints: The yo past of -ar verbs ends in -é: trabajé. Trabajo is present, trabaja another person's present, trabajar the infinitive — only trabajé is the done-and-dusted I-form.
activities.feedback: trabajé — the é is the I-did-it marker. trabajo is present (I work), trabaja is he/she present, trabajar is the untouched infinitive.

activities.prompt: Predict the yo past of comer: Yesterday I ate → Ayer ___ .
hints: Comer is an -er verb, so the yo past ends in -í: comí. The accent is part of the spelling.
activities.feedback: -er/-ir verbs take -í for yo: comí. Keep the accent — comi without it is a spelling mistake, not a past tense.

errors.explanation: The yo past carries its accent: comí.
Como is the present 'I eat'; yesterday needs the past comí.
Comer is the infinitive; the sentence needs the conjugated past form comí.

activities.prompt: Estuvo enfermo ayer. Which verb is the rebel here?
hints: Estuvo is estar's past — it ignores the -ar pattern completely, so it is the rebel. Enfermo is an adjective, ayer a time word, and fue is not even in the sentence.
activities.feedback: estuvo — estar's past ignores the -ar pattern completely (no *estó). enfermo is an adjective, ayer a time word, and fue isn't even in the sentence.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: We ate paella on Sunday.
hints: Verb first, then what, then when: Comimos paella el domingo. The past verb Comimos leads the whole sentence.
activities.feedback: Comimos paella el domingo — verb first, then what, then when. The past verb carries the whole sentence.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: He told me no.
hints: Decir's past is dijo ('he told'), and the que links the telling to the 'no': Me dijo que no. Me dije would be 'I told myself'.
activities.feedback: decir → dijo in the past — one of the rebels. Me dijo que no: told-me that no.

errors.explanation: The told-me-that-no bridge needs que: Me dijo que no.
Dije is 'I said'; the prompt says 'he told me' — Me dijo que no.
Decía is the habit-tense; a single 'he told me' takes dijo: Me dijo que no.

activities.prompt: Anoche ___ la tarea. (hacer, yo)
hints: Hacer's yo past is the rebel hice — no pattern, just a friend to memorize: Anoche hice la tarea.
activities.feedback: hacer → hice. The yo past of hacer drops the pattern — memorize hice the way you memorized fue.

errors.explanation: Hago is the present 'I do'; anoche calls the past hice.
Hizo is 'he/she did'; the prompt says yo — hice.
Hacía is the habit-tense; a done-and-dusted task takes hice.

activities.prompt: Read the day. What time did the narrator get home?
hints: The story's last sentence gives it: llegué a casa a las once. The time is a las once — not the seven o'clock of getting up.
activities.feedback: Llegué a casa a las once — the last pretérito of the story, and your answer.

errors.explanation: Seven was when the narrator got UP; home came at a las once.
Friends were the dinner company; the question asks the time he got home — a las once.
The report was finished in the afternoon; getting home happened a las once.

activities.body: Before rules, feel the difference: Habló = he spoke, done. Hablaba = he was speaking, ongoing. The imperfecto is the movie camera — era, iba, jugaba paint the scene while the action happens. The forms are kind: -ar verbs take -aba (hablaba), -er/-ir verbs take -ía (comía, vivía), and there are only three rebels in the whole tense: era, iba, veía.

activities.prompt: Which sentence describes a habit in the past?
hints: The album's first caption is the model: de niño jugaba = 'used to play', the stretched habit. Ayer jugué snaps it shut (pretérito), and the present forms (juego, mañana juego) are the wrong time.
activities.feedback: jugaba = used to play, the habit. jugué = played once and done; juego = present. Only the imperfecto stretches time into a habit.

activities.prompt: Predict the imperfecto of ser (he/she was, setting the scene).
hints: Ser is one of the three irregular imperfectos the intro named — era, iba, veía. Era paints the scene; the pretérito fue would snap it shut.
activities.feedback: era — one of only three irregular imperfectos (era, iba, veía). Everything else follows -aba/-ía.

errors.explanation: Fue is the pretérito — snapped shut. The imperfecto stretches the scene: era.
Es is the present; the scene-setting past of ser is era.

activities.prompt: Which is NOT a regular imperfecto form?
hints: The movie camera wears -aba and -ía — scan the endings: hablaba, comía and vivía all fit the pattern, while habló carries -ó, the pretérito's snapping ending. It is the odd one out.
activities.feedback: habló is pretérito — the -ó ending snaps the action shut. The -aba/-ía endings are the imperfecto's signature.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: There were many people in the square.
hints: The frozen photo used había — the imperfecto of hay — and it stays singular even for many people: Había mucha gente en la plaza.
activities.feedback: había — the imperfecto of hay, for there-was scenes. No plural form: había covers many people too.

answers: Había mucha gente en la plaza.

errors.answer: Hay mucha gente en la plaza.
errors.explanation: Hay is the present; the past scene takes había.

errors.answer: Hubo mucha gente en la plaza.
errors.explanation: Hubo is the pretérito — a finished moment. The background scene takes había.

errors.answer: Había mucha gente en el plaza.
errors.explanation: Plaza is feminine: la plaza.

activities.prompt: De niño, ___ al fútbol todos los días. (jugar, yo)
hints: De niño + todos los días spells habit, and the prompt conjugates it for yo: jugar → jugaba — the very form that opened the album.
activities.feedback: De niño + todos los días = habit → imperfecto: jugaba. The time words decide the tense.

errors.explanation: Jugué is the pretérito — a finished game. 'Every day' needs the stretched habit: jugaba.
Juego is the present; the habit lives in the past: jugaba.
Jugo means 'juice' — the imperfecto is jugaba, keeping the -aba the camera uses.

activities.body: The future is the kindest tense in Spanish: don't touch the infinitive, just add endings — hablaré, comeré, viviré. One pattern for all three verb groups: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -án. Then learn the six rebels that change their stem — tendré, podré, haré, diré, vendré, saldré — and you own tomorrow.

activities.prompt: How is the simple future formed?
hints: The future touches nothing: infinitive + endings. Hablar + é = hablaré — no stem change and nothing removed. -aba is the imperfecto, not the future.
activities.feedback: infinitive + endings: hablar + é = hablaré. -aba is the imperfecto; the infinitive stays whole — nothing is removed.

activities.prompt: Predict the yo future of comer.
hints: comer + é = comeré. The future uses the same endings for every verb group — comer keeps its full infinitive.
activities.feedback: comer + é = comeré. Same ending for -ar, -er and -ir — the future doesn't care about verb groups.

errors.explanation: The yo future carries its accent: comeré.
Comía is the imperfect habit-tense; the future of comer is comeré.
Comer is the infinitive; the future yo form keeps it and adds -é: comeré.

activities.prompt: Which verb keeps a normal stem in the future?
hints: Hablar keeps its stem — hablaré is the regular one. Tendré, podré and diré all trade in new stems; only hablaré follows the pattern.
activities.feedback: hablaré — hablar is regular. tener→tendré, poder→podré and decir→diré are three of the six rebel stems.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: Tomorrow I will speak with him.
hints: When comes first — Mañana — then the future verb hablaré, then with whom: con él. Mañana hablaré con él.
activities.feedback: Mañana hablaré con él — when, what, with whom. The future verb carries the promise.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: We will eat at two.
hints: comer + emos = comeremos ('we will eat'), then the time with its las: a las dos. The nosotros ending stresses its own first syllable.
activities.feedback: comer + emos = comeremos. The nosotros ending is the only one with the stress on the ending's first syllable.

errors.explanation: Comemos is the present 'we eat'; the plan wears the future: Comeremos a las dos.
The clock time needs its las — 'at two' is a las dos.
Comeré is 'I will eat'; the prompt says 'we' — Comeremos a las dos.

activities.prompt: El viernes ___ a cenar. (salir, nosotros)
hints: Salir is one of the six rebels: the stem becomes saldr-, and nosotros ends in -emos: saldremos.
activities.feedback: salir → saldr-: saldremos. The d sneaks in — one of the six rebels.

errors.explanation: Salimos is the present 'we leave'; the week ahead needs the future saldremos.
Saldrá is 'he/she will leave'; the prompt says nosotros — saldremos.
Regular future would be saliremos, but salir is a rebel: its stem is saldr-, so saldremos.

activities.prompt: Read the week ahead. When will the narrator travel to Barcelona?
hints: The first lines map the week: el lunes tendré una reunión, el martes viajaré a Barcelona. The Barcelona trip wears martes, not the meeting's lunes.
activities.feedback: el martes viajaré — the future verb plus its day. Plans wear dates.

errors.explanation: Monday holds the meeting; the trip to Barcelona is on martes.
Wednesday holds the presentation; Barcelona is on martes.
Friday is the celebration dinner; the Barcelona trip is on martes.

activities.body: The future isn't just tomorrow — it does three jobs. It promises: Te llamaré esta noche. It predicts: Mañana lloverá. And it wonders about right now: ¿Dónde estará? — where can he be? Watch for creo que, probablemente, seguro and quizá — they turn plain statements into forecasts.

activities.prompt: ¿Dónde estará? — What is the future doing here?
hints: The fortune teller isn't forecasting tomorrow here — estará wonders where he is right now. The intro named it the future's third job: a guess about the present.
activities.feedback: guessing about now — estará wonders where he is at this moment. The future of supposition isn't about tomorrow at all.

activities.prompt: Predict: there will be sun → ___ sol.
hints: Haber's future stem is habr-, and the -á ending makes 'there will be': habrá. The intro's examples — habrá gente, habrá tiempo — all use this one form.
activities.feedback: haber → habrá — the future of there-is. Habrá sol, habrá gente, habrá tiempo.

errors.explanation: Hay is the present 'there is'; the prediction needs the future habrá.
Habría is the conditional ('there would be'); for 'there will be' the future is habrá.
The future form carries its accent: habrá.

activities.prompt: Te llamaré esta noche is a…
hints: Te llamaré commits the speaker to actually calling — the future's promising job, the fortune teller's very first line. Predictions forecast weather; guesses wonder about now; habits live in the past.
activities.feedback: promise — te llamaré commits the speaker. Predictions need a forecast (lloverá); guesses wonder (estará).

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: I think it will rain tomorrow.
hints: Open with the booster creo que, pull the weather verb into the future — lloverá, with its accent — and drop mañana: Creo que lloverá mañana (or Creo que mañana lloverá).
activities.feedback: Creo que turns lloverá into a personal forecast. Prediction + booster = natural Spanish.

errors.explanation: Llueve is the present; the forecast needs the future lloverá.
The infinitive llover needs its future ending: lloverá.
The future form carries its accent: lloverá.

activities.prompt: ___ que vendrá. (I think…)
hints: The prompt hands you the meaning — 'I think' — and the que after the blank is already written. The lesson's booster is creo: Creo que vendrá.
activities.feedback: Creo que vendrá — I think he will come. The booster softens the prediction into an opinion.

errors.explanation: Cree is 'he/she thinks'; 'I think' is creo: Creo que vendrá.
The que in the sentence is already written — the blank holds just Creo: Creo que vendrá.
Pienso que is grammatical Spanish, but this lesson models the booster creo: Creo que vendrá.

activities.body: Decided plans don't wear the future tense — they wear ir a: Voy a estudiar medicina, vamos a comprar una casa. The decision is made; the ticket is bought. Add querer for the wish behind the plan: Quiero aprender italiano. Plan first with ir a, wish second with querer.

activities.prompt: Which sentence states a decided plan?
hints: Ir a carries a decided plan: Voy a estudiar medicina. Quizá is a maybe, estudiaba a past habit, estudié a finished past — none is a live plan.
activities.feedback: Voy a = decided and happening. quizá = maybe; estudiaba = used to; estudié = finished. Only ir a carries a live plan.

activities.prompt: Predict: you (tú) are going to come → ___ a venir.
hints: Ir hands tú the form vas; the a is the bridge and the second verb stays untouched: vas a venir.
activities.feedback: ir gives vas for tú — vas a venir. The a is the bridge; the second verb never changes.

errors.explanation: Voy is 'I am going'; the prompt says you (tú) — vas.
Va is he/she; you-tú is vas a venir.
Vamos is 'we'; the prompt asks for tú — vas.

activities.prompt: Vamos a comprar una casa. Who is 'we'?
hints: Vamos ends in -amos, the nosotros giveaway: we. The plan includes the speaker — that is the 'we'.
activities.feedback: vamos = we (nosotros) — the plan includes me. The ending -amos is the giveaway.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order: I am going to learn Italian.
hints: Conjugated ir first — Voy — then the bridge a, then the untouched infinitive aprender, then what: italiano. Voy a aprender italiano.
activities.feedback: Voy a aprender italiano — conjugated ir, then a, then the untouched infinitive. That order never changes.

activities.prompt: Translate into Spanish: We are going to travel in summer.
hints: We-plan = vamos + a + the infinitive: vamos a viajar. Then en verano pins the season. The bridge a never disappears.
activities.feedback: Vamos a viajar — we-plan in four syllables. En verano pins down when.

errors.explanation: Ir a needs its bridge a: Vamos a viajar en verano.
Only the first verb conjugates — after a comes the bare infinitive: vamos a viajar.
Voy is 'I'; the prompt says 'we' — Vamos a viajar en verano.

activities.prompt: ___ a venir a la fiesta? (tú, are you going to…)
hints: The invite checks the other person's plan: tú goes with vas. Vas a venir a la fiesta? — not voy.
activities.feedback: ¿Vas a venir? — the invitation check. Vas, not *voy: the plan is theirs, not yours.

errors.explanation: The plan is yours, not mine — tú takes vas: ¿Vas a venir a la fiesta?
Va is he/she; the question asks tú — vas.
Vamos is 'we'; the question asks you — vas.

activities.prompt: Read the life plan. Who is going to live with the narrator?
hints: The passage's third sentence: Mi hermana va a venir a vivir conmigo. The sister moves in — the new job and the Italian are separate plans.
activities.feedback: Mi hermana va a venir a vivir conmigo — va a, the third-person plan.

errors.explanation: The narrator is going to LOOK FOR a new job — the one moving in is the sister: mi hermana.
No mother appears here. The passage says mi hermana va a venir a vivir conmigo.
Summer is when they travel together; the person coming to live is her sister.

activities.prompt: ¿Podrías ayudarme? This is…
hints: Podrías is poder wearing the conditional — the would-you form that softens a request. A past event would be podías or pudiste; a command drops the conditional.
activities.feedback: a polite request — the conditional softens could you into asking, not telling. Commands bark; the conditional knocks.
